## Author's thesis (paraphrased from source)

Marketing is an applied management discipline whose object is the creation, communication, delivery, and exchange of offerings that have value for customers, partners, and society at large. The text adopts the American Marketing Association definition early and pivots to a working definition: marketing is "every process involved in moving a product or service from the organization to the consumer" — discerning customer needs, developing offerings to meet them, identifying likely buyers, promoting, distributing [V] (Ch 1.1, "Marketing Defined"). The book's organising premise is the **marketing mix** — the 4Ps of *product, price, place, and promotion* — coupled with the explicit elevation of *value* as both the customer's evaluation criterion and the company's strategic outcome [AP] (Ch 1.2, "Marketing Mix Defined").

A second load-bearing claim is that customer-driven (rather than product-driven) strategy is the contemporary norm: companies start with prospective consumers' needs and wants and then build offerings to satisfy them [AP] (Ch 1.1, "Step 2: Develop a Customer-Driven Marketing Strategy"). The text traces this as the historical endpoint of an evolution — production concept (post–Civil War to 1920s), product concept (1920s–1950s), sales concept (post-1950s), marketing concept, and societal marketing concept — with the societal concept extending the marketing concept to include long-term societal welfare [AP] (Ch 1.4, "The Evolution of Marketing").

A third load-bearing claim is that **segmentation, targeting, and positioning (STP)** is the spine of customer-driven strategy: "you can't be all things to all people," so marketers segment broad markets into subgroups, select targets where their resources can produce profitable response, and position offerings in customers' minds against competitors [V] (Ch 5.1, "Market Segmentation Defined"; Ch 5.6, "Product Positioning Defined"). Positioning, drawing on Ries and Trout, is "not to create something new and different, but to manipulate what's already up there in the mind" [BT] (Ch 5.6, "Product Positioning Defined").

A fourth load-bearing claim is that **integrated marketing communications (IMC)** beats fragmented promotion: marketers should combine advertising, sales promotion, personal selling, public relations, direct marketing, and digital/Internet marketing into a unified, consistent message across channels because "consumers are bombarded with marketing messages throughout the day" [V] (Ch 13.1, "The Importance of the Promotion Mix") — an estimated 5,000 ads per day per digitally connected person (Ch 13.1, "What Is the Promotion Mix?") — and a single channel rarely cuts through [AP] (Ch 13.1, "The Importance of the Promotion Mix"; Ch 13.3, "Integrated Marketing Communications").

A fifth load-bearing claim, presented as the "new paradigm" in the closing supplemental chapter, is that **sustainable marketing** is now a business imperative: "an organization should meet the needs of its present consumers without compromising the ability of future generations to fulfill their own needs" [BT] (Ch 19.1, "Environmental Sustainability", attributed to Philip Kotler). The text frames sustainability through three pillars — environmental, social, economic (governance) — paralleling the ESG (environmental, social, governance) reporting framework (Ch 19.1, "Environmental Sustainability"; Ch 19.2, "Differences between Traditional and Sustainable Marketing").

The book is pedagogically organised: every chapter opens with an "In the Spotlight" company case, names learning outcomes per section, dedicates an explicit ethics section per chapter, and includes a "Marketing Plan Exercise" cumulative project across chapters.

## Part I: Marketing fundamentals — value, the marketing mix, and the marketing environment (Ch 1)

### What marketing is and the five-step marketing process

Marketing can also be defined as identifying and anticipating customer needs and then satisfying them profitably [AP]; in marketing terms, "the road to profitability means adding value to a product so that the price customers pay is greater than the cost of making the product" [V] (Ch 1.1, "Marketing Defined").

The section's Marketing in Practice feature, "Reconciling Segmentation and Diversity", sets two pressures against each other [AR]. As the consumer population diversifies, diversity, equity, inclusion, and belonging (DEIB) is "no longer the “right” thing to do; rather, it’s imperative" [V], so brands must authentically reflect a wide range of backgrounds and life experiences, respect individual preferences and promote customisation [AP]. Yet profitable production needs market segmentation, which "requires assigning individuals to predefined categories with predictable behaviors, based on standardized assumptions" [V]. The box asks how segmentation differs from stereotyping and how it can support diversity, points to three articles, and defers the question to the book's chapters on segmentation and on the diverse marketplace [AP] (Ch 1.1, "Reconciling Segmentation and Diversity").

**Interested parties** are "those persons or entities that have an interest in the success or failure of a company" [V], and "You may see these people and groups referred to as “stakeholders” in business writing and other media" [V]. Internal interested parties are employees, owners, managers, and investors (shareholders); external interested parties are customers, creditors, suppliers, distributors, and society at large, who have no direct say in the company's decision-making but on whose support its success depends [AP] (Ch 1.1, "How Marketing Benefits the Organization, Its Interested Parties, and Society"). **Internal marketing** "involves promoting the objectives, products, and services of a company to its internal constituents—particularly employees" [V]; its benefit shows in "employees who are motivated and empowered to deliver a satisfying customer experience" [V] (Ch 1.1, "How Marketing Benefits the Organization, Its Interested Parties, and Society").

The text presents marketing as both a set of activities (promotion, distribution, exchange) and a process. The **marketing process** is "the series of steps that assist businesses in planning, analyzing, implementing, and adjusting their marketing strategy" [V] (Ch 1.1, "The Marketing Process Defined"). The book uses a five-step version: (1) understand the marketplace and customers; (2) develop a customer-driven marketing strategy; (3) deliver high customer value; (4) grow profitable customer relations; (5) capture customer value in the form of profits [AP] (Ch 1.1, "Steps in the Marketing Process").

**Customer value** is defined as "the ratio between the perceived benefits and costs incurred by the customer in acquiring your products or services" [V] (Ch 1.1, "Step 3: Deliver High Customer Value"). Value is decomposed into four types: functional, monetary, social, and psychological [AP] (Ch 1.1, "Step 3: Deliver High Customer Value"). **Customer equity** — the potential profits a company earns from its current and potential customers — is presented as the bellwether of financial success and the consequence of customer loyalty [AP] (Ch 1.1, "Step 5: Capture Customer Value").

The book introduces its recurring Careers in Marketing feature with "Marketing Jobs", which says each chapter's box outlines job roles, day-to-day work, qualifications and sometimes salary [AP]. It advises readers who want a marketing job to learn what roles exist and what each expects, to seek out the insights of people in those roles and perhaps connect with them, and to work out what they like doing, what they are good at, and how to build a network; it lists five web resources on entry-level careers and salaries and calls marketing "a creative, interesting, and at times exciting role where you can make a real impact on people’s lives" [V] (Ch 1.1, "Marketing Jobs").

### The 4Ps of marketing

The **marketing mix** is "commonly referred to as the tactics a company can use to promote its products or services in the market in order to influence consumers to buy" [V] (Ch 1.2, "Marketing Mix Defined"). Its four elements:

- **Product** — the good or service the company provides.
- **Price** — what the consumer pays in exchange.
- **Place** — where the product is purchased.
- **Promotion** — advertising, sales, and other communications used to attract the customer (Ch 1.2, "The 4Ps of Marketing").

The text also introduces an internal counterpart, the **5Ms of marketing** (sometimes called the 5M framework): minds (staffing), minutes (time), machinery (equipment), materials (production), money (finance) — internal organisational assets that must be addressed for any marketing strategy to succeed [AP] (Ch 1.3, "Components of the Internal Environment").

A Link to Learning feature, "Netflix, JanSport, and Stranger Things", gives a real-world promotion example: a brand partnership in which the two companies launched Stranger Things–branded backpacks with the show's fourth season in 2022, five Hawkins-inspired designs on Stranger Things themes [AE] (Ch 1.2, "Netflix, JanSport, and Stranger Things").

### The marketing environment: micro, macro, and PESTLE

The **marketing environment** comprises both internal and external factors that influence an organisation's marketing decisions [AP] (Ch 1.3, "The Marketing Environment Defined"). The internal environment is structured by the 5Ms and organisational culture. Zappos is the text's positive-culture example: its "call-center employees are empowered to do “whatever it takes” to make the customer happy" [V], use no scripts for calls, and have no time limits on calls (Ch 1.3, "Components of the Internal Environment"). The external environment splits into the **microenvironment** — five factors the firm interacts with directly: suppliers, market intermediaries, customers, competitors, the general public — and the **macroenvironment**, captured by the PESTLE acronym: Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal, Environmental factors [AP] (Ch 1.3, "Components of the External Environment"; "Components of the Macroenvironment").

In Ch 1.4's account of the product concept, a Link to Learning feature, "The Reckoning", adds that "When American cars developed a reputation for not being reliable or dependable, this opened an opportunity for Toyota and other Japanese exporters in the late 1960s and 1970s" [V], and points to David Halberstam's 1986 book *The Reckoning* and a 1986 New York Times review of it for more on the issue [AP] (Ch 1.4, "The Reckoning").

### Customer needs, the value proposition, and the exchange process

The text identifies five types of customer needs: stated, real, unstated, delight, and secret [AP] (Ch 1.5, "Identifying Consumer Needs and Wants"). A **value proposition** is "a promise of value that communicates the benefits of your company's products or services" [V] (Ch 1.1, "Step 2") — concretely, a brief statement compressing what the customer wants and how the offering meets it better than competitors. The **exchange process** is "the act of obtaining a desired product or service from an individual or business by providing in return something of value" [V] (Ch 1.5, "The Exchange Process"). The book carefully distinguishes **customer** (who purchases) from **consumer** (who uses) — the grandmother buying a toy is the customer; the grandson is the consumer (Ch 1.5, "The Exchange Process").

### Customer relationship management and ethical marketing

**Customer relationship management (CRM)** is "the means through which companies track, manage, and analyze customer interactions" [V] (Ch 1.6, "The Impact of CRM"). CRM systems are categorised as operational, analytical, or collaborative (Ch 1.6, "The Impact of CRM"). Loyalty programs are an industry-tested driver: "approximately 84 percent of customers indicate that loyalty programs are an incentive to remain with a brand, and 66 percent report that their spending behavior is actually altered by the ability to earn rewards" [V] (Ch 1.6, "Managing Customer Loyalty Programs"). "CRM isn’t a one-way communication street to customers. It’s a two-way street that allows customers to define and consequently shape offerings in terms of their requirements" [V] (Ch 1.6, "The Role of CRM in Building Customer Equity").

The text closes with **ethical marketing** as "a philosophy that tries to promote fairness, honesty, and a sense of responsibility" [AP] (Ch 1.7, "Ethical Marketing Defined"). Mintel research is cited: 56 per cent of US consumers stop buying from companies they believe are unethical [V] (Ch 1.7, "The Importance of Ethical Marketing"). The dos: ensure transparency (Southwest Airlines' "Transfarency" campaign); respect data privacy (Vizio's class-action suit over tracking viewing data without permission); prioritise consumer concerns and respond promptly (for an email to a company, "42 percent of consumers expect a response within 60 minutes and 32 percent expect a response within 30 minutes" [V]). The don'ts: overemphasise or exaggerate ("puffery"); make false or unverified claims (Living Essentials, maker of 5-Hour Energy, ordered to pay $4.3 million for misleading claims); make false comparisons about competitors' products, for which competitors can sue under the federal Lanham Act [AP] (Ch 1.7, "The Dos and Don’ts of Ethical Marketing").

The chapter closes with a Companies with a Conscience feature, "TOMS Shoes", drawn from a case study and the company's impact reporting [BT, Naeini; TOMS]. Blake Mycoskie founded TOMS in 2006 after a trip to Argentina, where he saw how people lived in impoverished areas, and built the company around giving: the “One for One” concept, under which "for every pair of TOMS shoes sold, the company donates another pair to a child in need" [V]. TOMS reported providing more than 95 million pairs of shoes to children in 82 countries. In 2011 it carried the model into eyewear, donating a portion of the profits from each sale to save or restore the eyesight of people in developing countries; its website says TOMS Eyewear has helped restore sight to more than 780,000 people [BT, TOMS] (Ch 1.7, "TOMS Shoes").

## Part II: Strategic planning, the marketing plan, and KPIs (Ch 2)

### The strategic planning process and SMART goals

**Strategy** is "the plans, actions, objectives, and goals that outline how the business is going to compete in its chosen markets given its portfolio of products or services" [V] (Ch 2.1, "Strategic Planning Defined"). The text distinguishes corporate-level strategy (entire business in multi-unit firms; **strategic business units (SBUs)**), business-level strategy (single operating unit), and functional strategy (HR, marketing, production) (Ch 2.1, "Strategic Planning Defined").

The five-step strategic planning process: vision statement, mission statement, gap analysis, objectives and goals, monitor progress (Ch 2.1, "Steps in the Strategic Planning Process"). **Vision statements** are forward-looking, inspirational, and aspirational; **mission statements** state why the business exists, in one to three sentences, and are either customer-oriented or product-oriented (Ch 2.1, "Step One: The Vision Statement"; "Step Two: The Mission Statement"). A **gap analysis** answers three questions: where are we now, where would we like to be, what's stopping us from getting there [AP] (Ch 2.1, "Step Three: Perform a Gap Analysis").

**Goals** are broad statements of desired outcomes (3–5 year horizon); **objectives** are specific action items (1 year or less). Both must be **SMART**: specific, measurable, attainable, realistic/relevant, time-bound [AP] (Ch 2.1, "Step Four: Establish Objectives and Goals"). A **marketing dashboard** summarises key metrics into easy-to-read indicators for ongoing monitoring (Ch 2.1, "Monitor Progress").

The section's Careers in Marketing feature, "Marketing Manager", says the job differs by company and industry, but "in general it’s a leadership position in charge of the marketing strategy at a company or for a product" [V]. Marketing managers often carry out research, set pricing parameters, and work with finance, legal, advertising, promotion and product development, and they need to be proficient in problem-solving [AP]. The box cites a US Bureau of Labor Statistics projection of 10 per cent growth in the role from 2021 to 2031 [BT, US Bureau of Labor Statistics], and notes that many people move between marketing roles, carrying the skills of each into the next [AP] (Ch 2.1, "Marketing Manager").

### Portfolio analysis: BCG matrix and SWOT

The **BCG matrix** plots SBUs by market share (high/low) and market growth rate (high/low) into four cells: stars (high share, high growth), cash cows (high share, low growth), question marks (low share, high growth, "problem children"), and dogs (low share, low growth) [AP] (Ch 2.2, "Boston Consulting Group (BCG) Matrix"). The Apple worked example places iPhone as star, iPad and MacBook as cash cows, iWatch as question mark, iPod as dog (Ch 2.2, sample matrix).

A **SWOT analysis** maps strengths, weaknesses (internal, controllable), opportunities, threats (external, uncontrollable) onto a four-quadrant grid (Ch 2.2, "SWOT Analysis"). The book recommends ranking factors by competitive importance (strengths/weaknesses) and by likelihood and magnitude (opportunities/threats) (Ch 2.2, "SWOT Analysis").

### Growth strategies

Four generic growth strategies: market penetration (existing products, existing markets), product development (new/improved products, existing markets), market development (existing products, new markets), product diversification (new products, new markets) [AP] (Ch 2.2, "Strategy"). A market development strategy "involves searching for new market segments and uses for a company’s products" [V]. The text runs all four through one company, Harley-Davidson: penetration would sell more Harley-Davidson motorcycles in the US; product development would sell a new product such as children's biker clothing under the brand in the US; its current market development strategy is to develop a new motorcycle to manufacture and sell in China; diversification might sell new products like children's biker clothing in China [AP] (Ch 2.2, "Strategy"). Diversification splits into concentric (similar products to existing line), horizontal (new but unrelated products to existing customers), and conglomerate (significantly unrelated new products) (Ch 2.2, "Product Diversification").

### The 12-element marketing plan and KPIs

The text adopts a 12-element marketing plan: executive summary, mission statement, SWOT analysis, objectives and issues, market segmentation and target market, buyer personas, positioning, current marketing situation, marketing strategy, action programs, budgeting, controls (Ch 2.3, "Structure of a Marketing Plan").

**Marketing metrics** are quantifiable values; **key performance indicators (KPIs)** are metrics tied directly to business objectives with targets and time frames [AP] (Ch 2.4, "Marketing Metrics Explained"). The text catalogues KPIs in four categories: business objective (total sales/revenue, new vs incremental sales, profitability via gross margin); sales/revenue generation (Average Revenue per Customer, new customer acquisition with CAC, customer retention rates); market share (category share, relative market share); customer support (CSAT, customer resolution rate, customer resolution time, customer lifetime value) (Ch 2.4, "Examples of Business Objective KPIs" through "Examples of Customer Support KPIs"). The **CLV** worked example (Table 2.1) computes lifetime value across four customer segments — millennial parents ($119,250), millennial singles ($215,250), working moms ($174,800), Gen Z emerging professionals ($66,400) — showing that CLV depends on annual profit per customer, average years retained, and CAC [AP] (Ch 2.4, CLV exercise).

The section's Marketing in Practice feature, "Classic Cleaners and Automated Reporting", draws on TBH Creative's case study and the company's own locations page [BT, TBH Creative; Classic Cleaners]. Classic Cleaners, a dry cleaning and laundry provider based in Indianapolis, Indiana, has 17 locations [BT, Classic Cleaners]; it had always struggled with the question of what its customers really wanted, and sought an easy way to use real-time marketing to track and measure results and make data-driven decisions. It hired TBH Creative to automate its reporting: setting up a marketing dashboard to monitor statistics and analytics, auditing which marketing efforts were effective, and improving its website [BT, TBH Creative]. General manager Steve Arnold explains the aim as tracking customers "so we could identify who our target customers are, what types of messaging resonates with them" [V] (Ch 2.4, "Classic Cleaners and Automated Reporting").

A Marketing Dashboard feature, "Customer Lifetime Value (CLV)", frames the Table 2.1 exercise above. It defines CLV as an estimate of "how much a single customer is worth to a company over their customer life span" [V]; because CLV is forward-looking, "it is an estimate, not a guarantee" [V]. CLV should exceed customer acquisition cost, the amount invested in attracting a new customer, and must be weighed with other costs such as cost of goods sold or cost to serve to judge whether customers are profitable; investing in existing customers (loyalty programmes, customer and user experience, social media) reduces the need for continual acquisition spending [AP]. The exercise adds that raising Gen Z retention from two years to eight would give that segment the highest CLV, at $270,400 [AE] (Ch 2.4, "Customer Lifetime Value (CLV)").

### Ethics in strategic planning

CSR is framed as an obligation to integrate social and environmental concerns into operations; it took hold in the United States only in the 1970s, fuelled in part by President George H. W. Bush's "thousand points of light" call [BT] (Ch 2.5, "Millennials and Generation Z"). Cited Nielsen survey: "66 percent of global consumers are willing to pay more for sustainable products" and "73 percent (nearly three out of four) of millennials indicated that they would be willing to pay extra for sustainable goods" [V] (Ch 2.5, "Millennials and Generation Z"). The Toyota unintended-acceleration case anchors the cost of cover-up: a $1.2 billion fine, "the largest criminal penalty imposed on a car company in US history" [V] (Ch 2.5, "Key Ethical Considerations"). The text introduces the **triple bottom line** — the three Ps of sustainability: people, planet, profits (Ch 2.5, "Brand Enhancement").

## Part III: Consumer buying behaviour (Ch 3)

### The buyer's black box and four buying behaviours

**Consumer buying behavior** is "the decisions and actions people undertake to buy products or services for personal use" [V] (Ch 3.1, "Consumer Markets Defined"). The **buyer's black box** (stimulus-response model) takes marketing stimuli (4Ps) and environmental stimuli (economic, legal/political, technological, cultural) into the consumer's mind — beliefs, attitudes, motives, perceptions, values — plus the buying decision process, and outputs choices about what, where, when, how often, how much (Ch 3.1, "The Buyer's Black Box").

Four buying behaviours, partitioned by involvement and brand differentiation:
- **Complex buying behavior**: high involvement, significant brand differences (e.g., new car).
- **Dissonance-reducing**: high involvement, little perceived difference; post-purchase dissonance ("buyer's remorse") common (e.g., flooring).
- **Habitual**: low involvement, little brand differentiation (e.g., milk).
- **Variety-seeking**: low involvement, significant brand differences; brand switching for variety's sake (e.g., tortilla chips) (Ch 3.1, "Types of Consumer Buying Behavior").

### Five families of influences

The text categorises influences on consumer buying behaviour into five families:

1. **Cultural factors** — culture, subculture, social class, gender (Ch 3.2, "Cultural Factors").
2. **Social factors** — family (orientation and procreation), reference groups with opinion leaders (now also social media influencers), roles and status (Ch 3.2, "Social Factors").
3. **Personal factors** — age and life cycle stage (with generational cohorts), economic situation, occupation, lifestyle, personality and self-concept. Generational breakdown: baby boomers 1946–1964; Gen X 1965–1979/80; millennials 1981–1994/96; Gen Z 1997–2012 (Ch 3.2, "Personal Factors").
4. **Psychological factors** — motivation (anchored by **Maslow's hierarchy of needs**: physiological, safety/security, belonging, esteem, self-actualisation), perception (and three perceptual processes: selective attention, selective distortion, selective retention), beliefs, attitudes (cognitive/affective/intentional components), learning (the Law of Effect: pleasant consequences increase repetition, unpleasant decrease) [BT] (Ch 3.2, "Psychological Factors").
5. **Situational factors** — environmental (lighting, music, smell), spatial, social situation of shopping, goal of the trip, timing, mood (Ch 3.2, "Situational Factors").

The text reports the LED-vs-fluorescent grocery study: shoppers bought 25 per cent more on the LED-lit side over a 21-week trial [V] (Ch 3.2, "Situational Factors"). It also reports the often-cited estimate that "the average person encounters between 6,000 and 10,000 ads every single day" [V] (Ch 3.2, "Psychological Factors"). Since no one can attend to all those competing stimuli, consumers attend only to those relevant to their wants and needs at the time and "screen out the rest. That’s the process known as selective attention" [V] (Ch 3.2, "Psychological Factors").

A Link to Learning feature, "Failures and Inspirations", holds that cultural factors play a major role in how best to market, citing "numerous examples of company efforts that failed because they did not reflect an understanding of the culture in a particular market" [V]: Starbucks in Australia, Coca-Cola and PepsiCo on first entering China, and 7-Eleven in Indonesia [AE]. Understanding why a failure happened can shift strategy toward possible success [AP], and the box turns to success stories: Run DMC's deal with Adidas, which opened the door for later artists, Rihanna's Fenty beauty line, Adobe's “When I See Black” ad and Bumble's “Find Me on Bumble” campaign [AE] (Ch 3.2, "Failures and Inspirations").

A Link to Learning feature, "Behind the Gender Differences", holds that gender differences lead to different buying behaviours, pointing to the Birchbox hair and skin care subscription service as one example and to an article on the reasons, which include purpose, experience and brain make-up [AP]. It then gives the counter-view: marketing expert Gaby Barrios argues in a TED Talk that targeting consumers by gender is bad for business [BT, Barrios]; further videos cover gendered packaging decisions and their cost to consumers, and how fashion brands' parent companies use gender strategies (Ch 3.2, "Behind the Gender Differences").

A Marketing in Practice feature, "Marketing to the Ages", holds that knowing how to frame a message to a baby boomer versus a Gen Xer "is what makes marketers successful" [V], and points to articles on generational and age-agnostic marketing [AP]. It adds that "Nostalgia is an impactful tool in marketing because it gives a feeling of meaning and comfort" [V] (Ch 3.2, "Marketing to the Ages").

A Link to Learning feature, "Examples of Maslow’s Five Needs", pairs an advertisement with each level [AE]: Snickers' “You’re not you when you’re hungry” for physiological needs, Lysol's “What It Takes to Protect” for safety and security, an Ad Council public service announcement on belonging, Dove's campaign to boost female self-esteem (with “confidence-boosting boards” on Pinterest carrying self-esteem activities for girls and their parents) for esteem, and Nike's “Find Your Greatness” campaign for self-actualisation (Ch 3.2, "Examples of Maslow’s Five Needs").

A Marketing in Practice feature, "When Bombarding Backfires", warns that "Bombarding consumers with marketing messages can cause more harm than good" [V]: a Marketing Dive article reports that bombarding people with ads would hurt a brand [BT, Marketing Dive], Advertising Association data indicate that bombardment and intrusiveness hurt perceptions of advertising [BT, Advertising Association], and Quantcast outlines ways to avoid ad bombardment [BT, Quantcast] (Ch 3.2, "When Bombarding Backfires").

A Careers in Marketing feature, "It’s about Ability", applies the chapter to the reader's personal brand in a job search [AP]. Through Jason Shen's TED Talk it advises highlighting abilities rather than experience and telling one's story compellingly to potential employers [BT, Shen]; through the American Marketing Association it stresses self-knowledge of the work environment one performs best in and the work one enjoys most [BT, American Marketing Association]. It lists seven articles on standing out, and urges readers to contact current marketers (for example on LinkedIn) and work that research into the interview, because it "will speak to your drive, curiosity, and ambition" [V], with sample questions to ask them (Ch 3.2, "It’s about Ability").

A Marketing in Practice feature, "Lessons in Psychology", holds that insight into customers' thinking lets marketers create messages and stories that better speak to their needs, and calls learning, "the process where customers acquire information they can apply to future purchases" [V], a foundational concept in marketing, pointing to a Forbes article on types of learning [AP] (Ch 3.2, "Lessons in Psychology").

A Marketing in Practice feature, "Abercrombie & Fitch", shows smell and sound at work, drawing on a retail-marketing article [BT, Khan]. A&F sprays its own men's fragrance, “Fierce,” liberally in its stores to give off what it calls a "lifestyle . . . packed with confidence and a bold, masculine attitude" [V], so that male customers who want to smell like A&F identify with its models and sales staff; it also plays loud club music, which draws young people who can withstand it longer while older customers may run from it, helping it "maintain a more youthful clientele and a “fresher” image" [V]. A linked video covers how A&F positioned Hollister as a global teen brand and refocused A&F on young millennials [AP] (Ch 3.2, "Abercrombie & Fitch").

### Five-stage decision process and ethical consumerism

The **consumer decision process** has five stages: need recognition, information search (heightened attention or active search; internal/external/experiential), evaluation of alternatives (evaluating the "bundle of product attributes"), purchase decision (often using **heuristics** — mental shortcuts like price = quality, brand loyalty, country of origin), post-purchase evaluation (**cognitive dissonance** when uncertainty arises; satisfaction = function of expectations vs perceived performance) (Ch 3.3, "Consumer Decision Process").

A Careers in Marketing feature, "You Are Also a Consumer", points to resources on the five stages and to GWI's 2022 consumer trends report, which showed that consumers' needs and priorities have shifted [BT, GWI]. It invites readers to practise a personal needs assessment on themselves, since that self-awareness helps in finding a job that fits their interests and abilities, and lists free career aptitude and personality tests [AP] (Ch 3.3, "You Are Also a Consumer").

A Marketing in Practice feature, "Ethics and Corporations", notes that hundreds of companies are known for being ethical, including Patagonia, TOMS and Conscious Coffees, and points to lists of ethical companies and of ethical decisions that helped company brands [AE]. Because many consumers research companies before buying, it asks whether a company's ethical footprint shapes the reader's own purchasing (Ch 3.4, "Ethics and Corporations").

Ethical consumerism statistics cited: 90 per cent of US respondents would boycott a brand engaged in irresponsible business practices; 56 per cent would no longer do business with companies they perceive unethical; 72 per cent purchase from companies whose beliefs align with theirs on environment and child labour [V] (Ch 3.4, "Are You an Ethical Consumer?"). Consumers are "voting with their pocketbooks" [V]: they will take their business elsewhere if they perceive a disconnect between their values and the organisation's, and will likely share their sentiments on social media [AP] (Ch 3.4, "Are You an Ethical Consumer?").

A second Marketing in Practice feature, "Consumer Ethics", treats whether consumers care about ethics when buying as a hotly debated topic: some studies show interest in products that align with consumers' values and others show none, while research by Kellogg assistant professor of marketing Jacob Teeny, reported in Kellogg Insight, suggests that consumers care [BT, Teeny]. It points to a Jason Garman TEDx Talk on the power of choice and voice through purchasing [BT, Garman], and says the debate is growing with the increase of eco-friendly products, so marketers need to know it [AP] (Ch 3.4, "Consumer Ethics").

The chapter closes with a Companies with a Conscience feature, "Patagonia", drawn from a Vox article and a "Reasons We Love Patagonia" web page [BT, Baldwin; wearedore.com], which presents the maker of outdoor clothing gear for the “silent sports” as a leader in environmental and social responsibility [AR]. Its mission statement reads: "Build the best product, cause no unnecessary harm, use business to inspire and implement solutions to the environmental crisis" [V]. All its sewing production is fair-trade certified, and it publicly discloses all its first-tier suppliers and is mapping the rest down to farm level [BT, Baldwin]; a large share of its products are made from recycled materials or raw organic cotton (plastic soda bottles into fleece jackets, guayule plants into wetsuits), and it takes back worn-out products at no charge and recycles them into its supply chain [BT, wearedore.com] (Ch 3.4, "Patagonia").

## Part IV: Business markets and B2B buying behaviour (Ch 4)

The chapter's In the Spotlight opener presents RingCentral, a B2B provider of cloud-based business communications, which partnered with the customer feedback management platform Medallia: its product teams used direct customer feedback to drive feature innovation, and its sales and support teams used the same feedback to adjust training programmes and support processes [BT, Medallia]. After dashboards were rolled out, the support team reached an average customer satisfaction (CSAT) score of 9/10 in two key market segments; customer support director Chad Freeman credits "real time customer feedback and the opportunity to close the loop with the customer when the feedback is fresh" [V] [BT, Medallia] (Ch 4, "In the Spotlight").

### B2B vs B2C and types of B2B buyers

**B2B markets** differ from B2C on six dimensions, captured in Table 4.1: nature of the buying decision (organisational vs household); fewer buyers, higher volume; **derived demand** (B2B demand follows from B2C demand) vs **direct demand**; longer, more complex buying cycles; greater reliance on personal selling; geographical concentration (Ch 4.1, "Characteristics of the B2B Market"). Four types of B2B buyers: **producers** (transform inputs into other products), **resellers** (retailers, wholesalers, brokers — sell without material change), **government markets** (the largest single business and organisational market in the United States; require System for Award Management registration plus engagement with the General Services Administration and individual agencies), **institutions** (nonprofits, charities, churches, hospitals, universities) (Ch 4.2, "Types of Buyers").

The section's Marketing in Practice feature, "Alibaba", draws on Alibaba.com's own seller material [BT, Alibaba.com]. It presents Alibaba.com, founded in 1999 by Jack Ma, as an online B2B marketplace where buyers and sellers connect and transact, "sort of like a giant variety store for B2B buyers" [V], with hundreds of millions of products in over 40 categories and millions of sellers, likened to eBay in the B2C market [BT, Alibaba.com]. Its suppliers typically sell raw materials or manufactured goods to retailers, wholesalers, sourcing agents or manufacturers who source products to resell, and its Pay Later option, backed by Kabbage Funding, lets buyers purchase inventory without funds to hand and avoid more complicated financing [BT, Alibaba.com] (Ch 4.2, "Alibaba").

### Buy classes and the buying centre

Four **buy classes**, distinguished by newness, alternatives, uncertainty, and information requirements: **straight rebuys** (routine, standard, familiar supplier), **modified rebuys** (similar product but with one or more significant differences), **new-task buys** (first-time purchase; most complex), **systems selling/solution sale** (complete solution rather than separate components) [AP] (Ch 4.2, "Major Types of Buying Situations").

The **buying centre** (decision-making unit) has six roles: initiator, influencer (business and technical sub-types), gatekeeper, buyer (with authority to select suppliers and arrange terms), decider (final selection authority), user. Roles can overlap (Ch 4.2, "Participants in the B2B Purchase Process"). German research: 86 per cent of procurement decisions at large/medium companies involve groups of 2–20 people; companies under 100 employees average 3 people, those over 1,000 employees up to 34 people [V] (Ch 4.2, citing Gallup/Nink and Fleming).

### Influences on B2B behaviour and the eight-stage process

Five families of B2B influences: external (economic conditions, political/legal, competition, social environment); internal/organisational (business objectives and goals, technology, workforce skills); individual (age, education, job position, personality); interpersonal (expertise, organisational politics and culture); conditional (financial condition, product availability) (Ch 4.3, "Major Influences on B2B Buyer Behavior").

Eight stages in the B2B buying process: problem recognition, need description (developing the **bill of materials** — the recipe of parts), product specification (a blueprint), supplier search, proposal solicitation, supplier selection, order-routine specification (negotiating quantity, delivery, returns, warranties), performance review (Ch 4.4, "The B2B Buying Process").

### B2B ethics: bribes, FCPA, price fixing

The Transparency International Corruption Perceptions Index ranks 180 countries 0 (highly corrupt) to 100 (very clean); Denmark, Finland, New Zealand tied for first in 2021; the United States ranked 25th [V] (Ch 4.5, "Bribes and Grease Payments"). The **Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA)** (1977) prohibits bribes to foreign officials to obtain or retain business; enforcement is shared by SEC and Department of Justice (Ch 4.5, "The Foreign Corrupt Practices Act"). The 2019 StarKist canned-tuna price-fixing case is cited: $100 million fine [V] (Ch 4.5, "Price Fixing").

The section's Companies with a Conscience feature, "Kforce", draws on company and press sources [BT, Kforce; Huber; Anderson] and serves as the section's example of a company that shows ethics in B2B marketing [AP]. Kforce, a Tampa-headquartered B2B professional staffing and solutions firm specialising in technology, finance and accounting, with over 50 offices and two national recruiting centres [BT, Kforce], felt the impact of Hurricane Irma in 2017 on a personal level; the storm struck Florida as a Category 4 and knocked out power for more than 6.8 million people [BT, Huber]. The firm raised $1 million for the American Red Cross, sponsored private jet missions that flew essential supplies to the Bahamas and encouraged donations for hurricane relief [BT, Anderson]. In 2021 it widened its Day of Giving campaign into a Season of Impact, encouraging employees to give time and talents to nonprofits of their choice [BT, Kforce] (Ch 4.5, "Kforce").

## Part V: Segmentation, targeting, and positioning (Ch 5)

### Four bases for consumer segmentation

The text uses four primary bases:
- **Geographic** — location, cultural preferences, climate, language, population type/density (Ch 5.1, "Geographic Segmentation").
- **Demographic** — gender, income, age (with three sub-types: age range, life cycle stage, generation), education, race/ethnicity/religion, occupation, family structure (Ch 5.1, "Demographic Segmentation").
- **Behavioural** — benefit segmentation, occasion, usage rate (with the **Pareto principle**: 80 per cent of revenue from top 20 per cent of customers) (Ch 5.1, "Behavioral Segmentation").
- **Psychographic** — lifestyle (using the AIO model: activities, interests, opinions); personality variables; values; the **VALS framework** (innovators, thinkers, believers, achievers, strivers, experiencers, makers, survivors) (Ch 5.1, "Psychographic Segmentation").

**Multi-segment marketing** uses combinations (Ch 5.1, "Using Multiple Segmentation Bases").

The section's Careers in Marketing feature, "Market Research Analyst", describes the analyst as someone who studies markets and data to find potential new opportunities for a company [AP]. Citing the Bureau of Labor Statistics, it gives a bachelor's degree as the typical entry-level education and about 741,000 jobs, with expected growth of 22 per cent from 2020 to 2030 [BT, Bureau of Labor Statistics] (Ch 5.1, "Market Research Analyst").

### B2B segmentation

B2B segmentation is more complex than B2C because the buying centre is multi-personed and B2B buyers are more "rational" (deliberate, particularly on price), and B2B products are often integrated into larger systems and customised [AP] (Ch 5.2, "Challenges of Segmenting B2B Markets"). Five B2B segmentation methods: **firmographics** (industry, location, size, legal structure, performance — the B2B parallel to demographics); **technographics** (hardware/software stack); **needs-based** (Ted Levitt: "People don't want to buy a quarter-inch drill; they want a quarter-inch hole" [BT]); **value-based/tiering** (potential transactional worth); **behavioural** (interaction with company's website, content, marketing emails) (Ch 5.2, "Methods of Segmenting B2B Markets").

### International segmentation and Hofstede's dimensions

Four primary methods for international segmentation: geographic, political/legal, economic (developed/developing/underdeveloped), cultural (Ch 5.3, "Methods of Segmenting International Markets"). Hofstede "identified five dimensions that could be used to distinguish one culture from another"; "Four of these dimensions directly affect marketing in different cultures" [V]. Power Distance Index: "the United States has a moderately low PDI score of 40 on a scale of 1 to 100, compared to a world average of 55" [V]. Individualism versus Collectivism: "The United States has a very high individualism score of 91, compared to many Latin American countries such as Ecuador and Guatemala, which have single-digit individualism scores" [V]. Uncertainty Avoidance: "The UAI for the United States is 46, putting it into the moderate range compared to European nations like Italy (UAI of 75) and Poland (UAI of 93)" [V]. Masculinity/Femininity: Japan is the example of a high masculinity ranking, the United States and Canada of a low one [AP] (Ch 5.3, "Segmentation Based on Cultural Factors", citing Hofstede).

### ADAMS, target market strategies, and positioning

The five essential factors for effective segmentation form the acronym **ADAMS**: Accessible, Differentiable, Actionable, Measurable, Substantial (Ch 5.4, "Essential Factors").

Four generic target marketing strategies: **undifferentiated/mass marketing** (one mix for whole market — Coca-Cola, M&M's); **differentiated/segmented** (multiple targeted brands — Nike's women, young athletes, runners); **concentrated/niche** (single segment — LUSH eco-friendly cosmetics); **micromarketing** (drills further into individual customisation — Stitch Fix uses 85 data points per customer) (Ch 5.5, "Target Market Strategies").

The text separates the target market from the narrower **target audience**, the consumers expected actually to buy: a children's toy may target boys aged 6 to 12, while their parents, who buy the toy, are the target audience [AP] (Ch 5.5, "Target Markets Defined"). The section's Marketing in Practice feature, "LEGO", draws on a press source [BT, Dodge] to show the distinction at work. LEGO markets to parents as well as children and has made the brand "parent-approved by combining fun for children with an educational “twist.”" [V]: it brands its products as a route into STEAM (science, technology, engineering, the arts and mathematics), with websites offering education sets from preschool through middle school, tips for playful parenting with LEGO bricks and daily build challenges [BT, Dodge]. The feature concludes that parents want toys that are safe, fun and help children learn, and that LEGO has won over its target audience [AR] (Ch 5.5, "LEGO").

A **buyer persona** is a semi-fictional representation of an ideal customer: name, age, interests, media usage, finances, brand affinities. Best Buy used Buzz, Barry, Ray, and Jill as named personas (Ch 5.5, "Target Markets Defined"). LinkedIn cited: 3–8 buyer personas adequate for most cases [V] (Ch 5.5).

**Product positioning** is "the process of deciding and communicating how an organization wants its market to think and feel about a product or service" [V] (Ch 5.6, "Product Positioning Defined"). The **STP model** integrates segmentation, targeting, positioning. Two main approaches: **head-to-head positioning** (Avis vs Hertz: "When you're only No. 2, you try harder. Or else." [BT] — turned $3.2 million annual loss into $1.2 million profit, first profitable year in over a decade) (Ch 5.6, "Head-to-Head Positioning"); a Link to Learning feature adds Wendy's campaign claiming its beef is fresh, never frozen, set against competitors, particularly McDonald's [AE] (Ch 5.6, "Example of Head-to-Head Positioning"); **differentiation positioning** (Curves women's-only fitness rejected the typical health-club layout — created new demand instead of competing head-to-head) (Ch 5.6, "Differentiation Positioning"). A **positioning statement** answers "What experience do you want your customers to have with this product or service?" with template variants supplied (Ch 5.6, "Positioning Statements"). A **perceptual map** plots the brand and competitors on two **determinant attributes** to reveal positioning, identify gaps, and surface mismatch between intended and actual perception (Ch 5.6, "Perceptual Positioning Maps").

### Ethics in target marketing

Concerns: ethnic and racial profiling (Facebook ads sued by HUD for permitting ad targeting/exclusion by race, gender, religion); marketing to children (per APA, children under 7–8 cannot discern persuasive intent; CCFC findings on gender stereotyping; childhood obesity tripled since 1970s; Juul colourful packaging and flavours targeted adolescents); marketing to the elderly (prescription drug claims, "cure-all" COVID products); low-income targeting (high-APR cards, MLM schemes) (Ch 5.7, "Ethical Implications of Target Market Selection").

The section's Companies with a Conscience feature, "Subway", offers a counter-case to the harmful targeting of children: a company that "tried to get it right" [V]. Drawing on a press source [BT, Holloway], it reports that in 2014 Subway aligned itself with then First Lady Michelle Obama's Let’s Move! initiative, pledging $41 million over three years to promote a healthy-eating programme aimed at children under the slogan "Playtime: Powered by Veggies" [V], and teamed up with the Partnership for a Healthier America, a nonprofit that works with the private sector to advance the initiative's goals [BT, Holloway]. Subway's vice president of operations, Suzanne Greco, framed the campaign as building "upon our ongoing efforts to create better choices for families" [V] [BT, Holloway] (Ch 5.7, "Subway").

## Part VI: Marketing research and big data (Ch 6)

### Big data, the MIS, and information sources

**Marketing research** "is the function that links the consumer, customer, and public to the marketer through information" [BT] (Ch 6.1, "Marketing Research Defined", citing AMA). **Big data** is described by the three Vs — volume, velocity, variety — produced by point-of-sale systems, IoT devices, third-party research firms, social media, mobile location data, and surveys (Ch 6.1, "Big Data and the Marketing Information System (MIS)"). Cited NewVantage Partners 2021 survey: 96 per cent of Fortune-1000 executives reported success with big-data and AI programs, 99 per cent are pursuing new or existing big-data programs; estimated 2.5 quintillion bytes of data created daily worldwide [V] (Ch 6.1).

The section's Careers in Marketing feature, "Market Research Analysts", says market research analysts are needed in numerous industries and, citing the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, that the job outlook shows a much higher rate of growth than average [BT, Bureau of Labor Statistics] (Ch 6.1, "Market Research Analysts").

A **marketing information system (MIS)** collects, analyses, and reports findings from internal and external data (Ch 6.1, "Big Data and the MIS"). Information sources split into **internal data** (sales, promotions, prices, R&D, logistics — historic view), **external data** (customer surveys, competitor sites, news, social media — costly only in time), and **competitive intelligence** (information about competitors from the marketplace — relevant to all 4Ps) (Ch 6.2, "Describe the Different Categories of Marketing Information").

### Seven-step research plan

Seven steps: define the problem (with research question/objectives and **target population**); develop the research plan (primary vs secondary; **syndicated data** as a sub-type of external secondary; qualitative vs quantitative; four research types — exploratory, descriptive, experimental/causal with A/B testing, ethnographic); select data collection method (**observational** — personal, **unobtrusive observation**, **mechanical**; one-on-one interview; focus group of 8–12; **survey/questionnaire** by mail, phone, in-person, electronic — with strengths/weaknesses table); design the sample (census vs sample; sample frame and sampling unit; sample size; **probability** — simple random, stratified random; **nonprobability** — convenience, judgement); collect the data; analyse and interpret (mean, median, mode, frequency, cross tabulation, **verbatims** for qualitative); prepare the research report (Ch 6.3, "Steps in a Successful Marketing Research Plan").

A Link to Learning feature in the analysis step, "Infographics", describes the **infographic** as a graphical format that lets research results be taken in quickly [AP]. Pointing to an external infographic, it says a good one needs four components (data, design, a story and the ability to be shared) and is less valuable without all four, and that infographics are particularly advantageous online [AP] (Ch 6.3, "Infographics").

### Methods of quantifying research

Four classes: awareness (**unaided** vs **aided**); customer satisfaction score (CSAT, 0–100 per cent — 75–85 considered good, above 85 exceptional); customer acquisition cost (CAC); customer effort score (CES — ease of service experience) (Ch 6.3, "Methods of Quantifying Marketing Research"). Under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act, "approved by Congress in 1991, no calls can be made prior to 8:00 a.m. or after 9:00 p.m. in the recipient’s time zone" [V] (Ch 6.3).

### Ethics: deception, privacy, confidentiality

**Sugging** is selling disguised as research; the Insights Association Code of Marketing Research Standards prohibits it (Ch 6.4, "The Use of Deceptive Practices"). A Link to Learning feature introduces the Insights Association (IA) as an organisation devoted to the support and integrity of quality marketing research, which "protects and creates demand for the evolving insights and analytics industry" [V] [BT, Insights Association], and holds that a solid understanding of ethical practice is critical for any marketing professional [AP] (Ch 6.4, "The Insights Association"). **Confidential data** (researcher knows identity, doesn't share) vs **anonymous data** (no identifying info collected). DuckDuckGo is presented as an exception in the search industry: no user data tracking or selling (Ch 6.4, "Breaches of Confidentiality").

The section's Companies with a Conscience feature, "Gallup", draws on Gallup's own publications [BT, Saad; Khoury and Semykoz; Gallup]. It presents the Gallup Organization as a market research firm specialising in market sentiment, whose annual assessment of the honesty and ethics of professions put nursing top in 2021 [BT, Saad], and relays its finding that ethical standards need to "be at the core of an organization’s purpose, brand and culture" [V] [BT, Khoury and Semykoz]. The feature argues that a firm investigating so many topics must hold itself and its employees to a high ethical standard and complete each research step with diligence, which is why Gallup is recognised for ethically backed data [AR]. It closes with former US Secretary of Defense Chuck Hagel calling Gallup "truly an island of independence" [V] [BT, Gallup] (Ch 6.4, "Gallup").

## Part VII: Global marketing (Ch 7)

### Why and why not to enter global markets

Advantages: increased revenues, decreased competition (in some markets), faster growth, diversification of risk, disposal of surplus goods (e.g., losing-team Super Bowl apparel donated rather than landfilled). Challenges: understanding the business landscape; understanding target country business politics; differences in regulations and marketing (on advertising prescription medications to the general public, "the United States and New Zealand are the only countries where this type of marketing is allowed" [V]); cultural differences (Nivea "White Is Purity"; Gucci balaclava sweater similar to blackface) (Ch 7.1).

### Assessment: HBR's seven characteristics

Harvard Business Review's seven characteristics of firms that win globally (Quackenbos): attitude (priority), aptitude (knowledge/skills), magnitude (scope-capability fit), latitude (ability to adapt), rectitude (legal/ethical flexibility), exactitude (alignment with flexibility/ambiguity), fortitude (long-term commitment) [BT] (Ch 7.2, Table 7.1). Three income types: **consumer income**, **disposable income** (after tax), **discretionary income** (after necessities) — luxury marketers care about discretionary; consumer-packaged-goods marketers care about disposable (Ch 7.2, "Consumer Income and Purchasing Power"). **Shrinkflation** is presented as a way for companies to avoid raising prices during inflation — Charmin ultra-soft toilet paper went from 264 to 244 sheets per roll without a price increase [V] (Ch 7.2).

Trade regulation tools: **tariffs** (Japan ≈ 2.5 per cent on non-agricultural products, among the lowest); **quotas**; **embargoes** (US embargoes on Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Syria); **trade blocs** (USMCA, EU27 — 10 major blocs globally) (Ch 7.2, "Trade Regulations").

Sociocultural variables: lifestyles, stereotypes (Mattel's Shanghai Barbie store closed after two years — Chinese culture stresses educational toys; Delta giraffe-Ghana social media gaffe), law and politics, education, technology (Uganda: 16 million cell phones, only 1 million homes with electric lights; Charge Ko Technologies portable charging solutions), values, customs and cultural symbols, language, idioms, nuances ("Gerber" translates to "puke" in French; UK "biscuit" = US "cookie"). Even idioms can cause problems within and across languages and cultures: in 2022 the pop star Lizzo apologised for and re-released a song in which she had used a culturally insensitive word she had not known to be one when recording [BT, Cain] (Ch 7.2, "Analyzing Sociocultural Factors").

The section's Careers in Marketing feature, "Global Marketing Manager", says that as more companies do business internationally, the global marketing manager's role is "becoming more important" [V]. Global marketing managers work to understand what international markets need, the competition, rules and regulations, and local cultures and values, and use this to develop global marketing strategies that appeal to the local market [AP]; the feature closes with pointers to a career guide and a video (Ch 7.2, "Global Marketing Manager").

### Six market entry modes and three firm types

Six entry modes (least to most involved): exporting, franchising (McDonald's: ~$500K liquid assets, $45K franchise fee, $1.3–2.3 million total expected; Jazzercise: $1,250 one-time fee plus liability insurance), licensing, joint venture (Kellogg's + Wilmar International for China), strategic alliance (Uber + Spotify), foreign direct investment (Tesla Shanghai factory) (Ch 7.3, "Ways an Organization Can Enter").

Three firm types: international firm (any global involvement); multinational firm (centralised — Amazon HQ Seattle); transnational firm (high local responsiveness — McDonald's franchise approach) (Ch 7.3, "Forms of Global Competition").

### Global marketing mix

Marketing strategy: **standardized global** (Coca-Cola — same brand, name, and iconic cursive writing in white on red worldwide) vs **adapted global** (Netflix — country-specific content libraries) (Ch 7.4, "Adapting Marketing Strategies"). Three product strategies: **straight product extension** (no change); **product adaptation** (Nike Air Zoom HIIT shoe Australia-only; McDonald's India: 160+ stores, no pork or beef, separate vegetarian/meat kitchens, Maharaja Mac with corn-and-cheese patty); **product invention** (entirely new — e.g., non-electric cooling for Uganda) (Ch 7.4, "Product"). Coca-Cola slogan localisations across countries (Table 7.2 — India "Always the Real Thing"; Spain "Siente El Sabor"; Hungary "Kóstold meg az érzést"). The **whole channel** concept extends distribution thinking to all members in international channels including transportation; pirates off Somalia (the Captain Phillips story) are cited (Ch 7.4, "Place: Distribution Channels").

### Ethics: outsourcing, working conditions, child labour, bribery, dumping

Topics covered: outsourcing trade-offs (WhatsApp Russian outsourcing reduced costs); work standards (Xinjiang cotton; Nike, Apple, Levi's scrutiny); workforce diversity and equal opportunity; child labour (UN treaties; per-country minimum age standards); bribery and corruption (FCPA reiterated); **dumping** (selling exported goods below cost to drive out competition then raising prices to monopoly levels — illegal in US and many other countries) (Ch 7.5, "Identifying Ethical Issues").

The section's Companies with a Conscience feature, "Kao Corporation", draws on Ethisphere, a Kao news release and a press source [BT, Ethisphere; Kao; Gemeš]. Founded in Tokyo in 1887, Kao is a "16-time Ethisphere World’s Most Ethical Companies honoree" [V], honoured every year since Ethisphere began its recognition [BT, Ethisphere]. Its strategies aim for zero waste in making cleaning and health and beauty products: from leftover materials it developed Bio IOS, a sustainable cleaning-product ingredient, and its product development encourages refill packs [BT, Gemeš]. In 2022 Kao and Costco began testing foldable containers reusable as packing material in a Kanagawa Prefecture Costco warehouse [BT, Kao]; Kao plans to extend them to other warehouses and the wider industry, and stresses societal and environmentally friendly innovation, gender equality and universal product design [BT, Gemeš] (Ch 7.5, "Kao Corporation").

## Part VIII: Marketing in a diverse marketplace (Ch 8)

### Standardization vs adaptation; diversity marketing as adaptation

**Standardization** applies identical guidelines for uniformity (Apple iPhones look and work the same worldwide except for power adapters); **adaptation** adjusts offerings to specific groups (Ford Motor Company D4 platform shared across Ford and Lincoln models for cost) (Ch 8.1, "Standardization Strategy Defined"; "Adaptation Strategy Defined"). **Diversity marketing** is an adaptation strategy applied to cultural or demographic differences within a market (Nike By You shoe customisation extending appeal across ethnic and social preferences) (Ch 8.1, "Diversity Marketing").

The section's Link to Learning feature, "Nike and Diversity", cites eMarketer data placing Nike among the companies with the highest levels of diversity in their advertising [BT, eMarketer], and offers its campaigns as models for future marketers: the Emmy-winning You Can't Stop Us, You Can't Be Stopped, the Nike Unlimited You commercial, Nike By You, and Nike's diversity, equity, and inclusion strategy [AE] (Ch 8.1, "Nike and Diversity").

### Five diversity dimensions; multicultural and sociodemographic populations

The text uses five parameters: cultural/racial/ethnic; gender and sexual identity; generational; religion; disability (Ch 8.2, "Diversity Marketing Defined"). 2019 Adobe study: 61 per cent of consumers think diversity in campaigns is important; 38 per cent more inclined to trust brands with strong diversity in advertising [V] (Ch 8.2). Top Design Firms: 67 per cent of consumers would make repeat purchases from companies with diversity-marketing commitment [V] (Ch 8.2). Heat agency: high diversity scores → 83 per cent higher consumer preference [V]. Acknowledging consumers' differences and adopting tactics to meet each group's needs and preferences "validates individuals’ importance in the market" [V] (Ch 8.2, "Importance of Diversity Marketing"). Missteps are costly: PepsiCo's 2017 "Live for Now Moments Anthem" commercial featuring Kendall Jenner drew heavy backlash for trivialising the Black Lives Matter movement and was described as insensitive and offensive; PepsiCo defended it as not intended to be disrespectful, then withdrew the commercial (estimated to have cost $5 million to produce) and apologised [BT, Smith; Adams] (Ch 8.2, "Factors Impacting Diversity Marketing").

The section's Link to Learning feature, "Fenty Beauty", presents Rihanna's brand as diversity marketing done well: beyond lending her name, she developed products that widened diversity in the beauty business, among them a 40-shade foundation range and a wide range of sizes, and the brand made $100 million in sales in its first 40 days [AE]. The feature notes criticism of some suppliers' use of child labour and what its founder described as careless choices during a fashion show, but says the brand remains known for a more inclusive approach to beauty and clothing [AP]. The section later returns to it: when diversity marketing is done correctly, as Fenty Beauty did, "it can boost brand awareness, consumer engagement, and sales" [V] (Ch 8.2, "Fenty Beauty"; Ch 8.2, "Factors Impacting Diversity Marketing").

The text projects a US majority-minority population shift by the mid-2040s and "plurality nation" status by 2050 — no group with sizeable majority. Multicultural segments (2020 US Census): Hispanic 19 per cent (≈ 63 million; one of the fastest-growing groups; median age 29; 59 per cent of US population growth between 2010 and 2021); Black 14.2 per cent (≈ 46.9 million; 88.7 per cent increase in "in combination" identification since 2010 census); Asian 7.2 per cent (≈ 24 million; fastest population growth 2000–2019); Native American/Alaska Native 1.1 per cent single-race (3.7 million) and ≈ 2.9 per cent in combination (9.7 million) [V] (Ch 8.2, "Multicultural Populations"; Ch 8.4, sub-segments).

Sociodemographic segments: LGBTQIA+ (≈ 5.6 per cent of US adults, ≈ 14.4 million); generational (2020 Census counts: Silent 21.7M; boomers 70.6M; Gen X 65M; millennials 72.2M; Gen Z 67M; Gen Alpha 27.6M); socioeconomically disadvantaged (over 34 million people living in poverty in 2019); and consumers with disabilities — "This group represents an estimated 61 million Americans. About one in four adults lives with some type of disability" [V]; consumers with disabilities have traditionally been underrepresented in marketing, though studies show they are one of the largest sociodemographic market opportunities after baby boomers and other segments [AP] (Ch 8.2, "Sociodemographic Populations").

The section's Careers in Marketing feature, "Multicultural Marketing Director", says that with growing opportunities for multicultural marketing, demand for multicultural marketing directors is growing [AP]. It advises readers to research the skills hiring managers want, learn from marketing executives how marketers can foster diverse cultures, expand their networks to include diverse and inclusive leaders, and keep developing soft skills [AP] (Ch 8.2, "Multicultural Marketing Director").

### The cultural iceberg and Hofstede dimensions for marketing

Anthropologist Edward T. Hall's iceberg analogy: tangible/external aspects (traditions, music, language, artifacts, clothing, literature) above the waterline; intangible/internal (thought processes, assumptions, beliefs, interpretations) below — 90 per cent of mass beneath [BT] (Ch 8.3, "Tangible versus Intangible Culture"). Burger King's "Texican Whopper" campaign is the text's cautionary example: ads showing a tiny Mexican wrestler dressed in a poncho-style Mexican flag beside a tall American cowboy offended some Spanish-speaking customers and had to be redone; insights about the distaste for stereotypes and respect for the flag as a national symbol could have prevented it [AP]. The campaign "was a failure because the marketers lacked an understanding of the unseeable elements, or the internal and intangible aspects, of Mexican culture" [V] (Ch 8.3, "Tangible versus Intangible Culture", Figure 8.9).

The Hofstede dimensions are revisited from a multicultural-marketing angle: individualism vs collectivism (US Hispanic, Black, Asian populations lean collectivistic in varying degrees); high vs low power distance (smartphone ownership as social-status display; Hispanic and Black consumers higher smartphone use for online health and educational content); masculinity vs femininity (Black men higher masculinity orientation than non-Hispanic White and Hispanic counterparts); uncertainty avoidance (Hispanic, Black, Asian higher than non-Hispanic White); long-term vs short-term orientation (Asian populations rate extremely high long-term); indulgence vs restraint (Ch 8.3, "Values and Attitudes"). Hispanic, Black, Asian consumers more optimistic about reaching economic success than non-Hispanic White consumers; collectivistic-orientation drives family/community considerations in financial decisions (Ch 8.3, "How Culture Influences Diversity Marketing").

### Hispanic, Black, Asian identities; acculturation

**Cultural identity** is how a person identifies with a culture, ethnicity, or social group — a sense of belonging that influences thinking and actions (Ch 8.4, "Hispanic Identity"). Hispanic identity is strongly linked to heritage; 83 per cent of US Hispanic population belongs to five subethnicities (Mexican 62.2 per cent, Puerto Rican 9.5 per cent, Cuban 3.9 per cent, Salvadoran 3.9 per cent, Dominican 3.5 per cent) [V] (Ch 8.4, "Hispanic Identity").

The text distinguishes Hispanic (language-based — Spanish-speaking origin), Latino/Latina (location-based — Latin American family origin), Latinx (gender-neutral, with note that many Hispanic people dislike or find offensive). Black identity: Pew Research 2019 — nearly 75 per cent of Black people say race is at the centre of their identity [V] (Ch 8.4, "Black Identity"). McKinsey: growing Black population represents over $300 billion per year in unmet demand [V]. Asian: 6 origin groups account for 85 per cent (Chinese 24, Indian 21, Filipino 19, Vietnamese 10, Korean 9, Japanese 7 per cent); ~50 per cent of Asian consumers in the US watch TV in both English and an Asian language [V] (Ch 8.4, "Asian Identity").

**Acculturation** is "the process by which a person's family cultural patterns change because of direct and constant contact with a different culture" [V] (Ch 8.4, "The Acculturation Spectrum"). Bicultural consumers merge both cultures simultaneously. The degree of acculturation depends on birthplace, immigration status, community connections, and personal comfort level; "a person born in the United States to immigrant parents is more likely to be acculturated than unacculturated" [V] (Ch 8.4, "The Acculturation Spectrum"). Unacculturated Hispanic consumers are more likely to support brands advertising in Spanish — a sign of respect (Ch 8.4).

The Ch 8.6 Companies with a Conscience feature, "Culturally Sensitive and Socially Inclusive Marketing", draws on press and company sources [BT, Nittle; Coca-Cola Australia; Day]. It names multinationals such as Coca-Cola, Google, Unilever and Microsoft that, like P&G, focus their marketing on cultural sensitivity and social inclusion, and smaller players such as Bumble, Fenty Beauty and ThirdLove championing diversity as a core value "rather than just chasing a trend in marketing" [V] [BT, Nittle]. Coca-Cola is the case: the early-1970s "Hilltop" commercial showed people of different races and cultures bonding over the drink; "Share a Coke", launched in Australia in 2011, went viral and became a global success [BT, Coca-Cola Australia]; and the 2014 "America Is Beautiful" commercial, with seven young bilingual American women singing in different languages, drew criticism and boycotts from some and applause from others [BT, Day]. The feature closes: "That is what diversity marketing is all about" [V] (Ch 8.6, "Culturally Sensitive and Socially Inclusive Marketing").

## Part IX: Products, services, and product life cycle (Ch 9, 11)

### Product–service continuum and three levels of product

Pure product (computer) → service-product blend (restaurant) → pure service (marketing class) (Ch 9.1, "Products and Services Defined"). **Customer experience (CX)** integrates technology, marketing, sales, and customer service across all touchpoints — the Apple Store as canonical; brands with strong customer experience tend to have more loyal customers who become brand advocates [AP] (Ch 9.1, "Customer Experience").

The section's Marketing in Practice feature, "Netflix", draws on a CXL blog post [BT, Schneider] and says Netflix "has perfected the customer experience" [V]. Using technology as a driver, Netflix predicts viewing preferences with an algorithm, removing friction from the user experience and making the brand an essential part of customers' lives; such personalisation is common among companies that excel in customer experience [AP]. A three-step sign-up brings the customer into a viewing world built around them, and the algorithm weighs viewing history, genre, time of day, how long the user watched, devices streaming, rating history for similar content and users with similar preferences [BT, Schneider]; as it learns, the experience improves, building brand loyalty [AP] (Ch 9.1, "Netflix").

Four consumer-product classes: convenience, shopping, specialty, unsought (Table 9.1). Four business/industrial-product classes: raw materials, manufactured materials and parts, capital items, supplies and services (Ch 9.1, "Classifications of Business and Industrial Products").

Three levels of product: **core product** (what the customer is actually buying — convenience, ego, ease, flexibility); **actual product** (features, brand, quality, packaging, design); **augmented product** (warranties, customer service, support — e.g., Butterball turkey hotline) (Ch 9.1, "The Three Levels of Product").

The section's Careers in Marketing feature, "Product Marketer", defines the role: a product marketer, also known as a product marketing manager, "promotes a product and its features to a target market" [V]. The feature otherwise points to job descriptions, salary, skills and education guides, a Google product marketing manager's video and a mock interview (Ch 9.1, "Product Marketer").

### Product items, lines, mix; line filling and stretching

A **product item** is a specific good (Domino's hand-tossed pizza). A **product line** groups similar/complementary items (Domino's crusts: hand-tossed, crunchy thin, handmade pan, Brooklyn style, gluten-free). The **product mix** is everything the company sells; **line depth** (count within a line); **mix width** (count of lines) (Ch 9.2). **Product line filling** keeps competitors out by adding within an existing line. **Product line stretching**: down (Tesla Model 3 after Model S), up (Godiva gold collection), or both (Dell access/creator/gaming laptops) (Ch 9.2, "Product Line Filling and Product Line Stretching").

### Product life cycle and stage-specific strategies

Four stages: **introduction** (consumer awareness building, sales starting to grow, high marketing investment, low profitability); **growth** (rising sales, copycat entrants, less marketing investment per unit, more profitable); **maturity** (typically the longest stage; sales growth slows); **decline** (significant decrease in sales and profitability) (Ch 9.3). Products do not always traverse all stages linearly (fads), and pricing/promotion strategies differ by stage:

- Introduction: rapid skimming (high price, heavy promo); slow skimming (high price, low promo — Tesla initial launch); rapid penetration (low price, heavy promo — Old Navy $8 jeans 1994); slow penetration (low price, low promo).
- Growth: product improvement (OXO universal design); distribution expansion (Home Run Inn restaurant → grocery); promotion shift from awareness to preference (TikTok 2021).
- Maturity: market modification (Cheerios repositioned as heart-healthy for boomers); product modification (Chobani flip yogurt 2015).
- Decline: divest (Coca-Cola's New Coke 2002, after 17 years); harvest (smartphones as new models hit market) (Ch 9.4).

### Branding, brand equity, brand development

A **brand** is "an intangible asset with tangible value" — a feeling combining promotion efforts and consumer meaning [V] (Ch 9.5, "Branding"). **Brand value** is the financial asset (subjective, may be transactional); **brand equity** is the additional value a brand has over a substitute. Tide commands a price premium over similar laundry detergents — Kevin Lane Keller's brand-equity pyramid: identity → meaning → response (feelings/thoughts) → resonance; a Link to Learning feature calls Keller's model "a prevailing framework that scholars use to think about the concept of brand equity" [V] (Ch 9.5, "Benefits of Branding"; Ch 9.5, "Keller’s Brand Equity Model"). Three positioning bases: attribute (Taco Bell late-night cravings — easily replicable); benefit (Eggo convenience); value (Ford "Built Ford Tough" — most robust because linked to consumer beliefs) (Ch 9.5, "Building Strong Brands").

The section's Link to Learning feature, "Logos", points to Harley-Davidson's logos and asks what emotions the brand name and mark evoke, adding: "While marketing teams can influence how a brand is seen in the marketplace, consumers often define the brand" [V]. It also notes that the colours used in logos have meaning [AP] (Ch 9.5, "Logos").

Four ownership types: national, private-label, licensed (luxury brands license names to manufacturers like Luxottica), co-brand (Doritos Locos Tacos) (Ch 9.5).

The section's Marketing in Practice feature, "Trader Joe’s", draws on a business-review article and a customer-service blog [BT, Mallinger; Rossy; Wilkinson]. It argues that Trader Joe's turned the drudgery of grocery shopping into a customer experience: using the tenets of the Blue Ocean Strategy, it removed costly parts of the traditional grocery store that add nothing to the experience, such as a large footprint and overwhelming stock, and added Hawaiian shirts, friendly employees, interesting food and a much smaller store, becoming a cult brand with fan groups across the Internet [AR]. It built its culture by empowering its "crew members", interviewed for enthusiasm and cross-trained [BT, Mallinger; Rossy], puts its food front and centre on social media, and stocks about 10 per cent of the food of a normal supermarket, "making choices easier on the customer" [V] [BT, Wilkinson] (Ch 9.5, "Trader Joe’s").

The **brand development matrix** plots existing/new brand × existing/new product category: line extension, brand extension, multibrand, new brand (Ch 9.6, Figure 9.8). Four loyalty levels: switchers, shifting loyals, split loyals, hard-core loyals (Ch 9.6, "Brand Loyalty Levels"). Three brand-effectiveness metrics: brand lift (perception over time pre/post campaign), brand engagement (emotional identification — social metrics, time on site, subscriptions, bounce rate), brand preference (consumer behaviour — most predictive of sales) (Ch 9.6, "Metrics to Measure Brand Effectiveness").

### Packaging, environmental concerns, ethics

Packaging is not one of the 4Ps but is closely tied to product, place (shopper marketing), and promotion (Ch 9.7). Functional benefits: storage, convenience, safety (Tide Pods child-locked lid), usability. Perceptual benefits: status (Tiffany's "little blue box" — its blue is trademarked) (Ch 9.7). McKinsey: more than half of US consumers highly concerned about packaging environmental impact (Ch 9.8). **Cradle-to-cradle packaging design** removes waste from the package's life cycle: regenerative, mimics nature; biological cycle (compostable) and technical cycle (regenerable resources) (Ch 9.8, Figure 19.15).

### Services characteristics and quality models (Ch 11)

Four service characteristics: **intangibility** (cannot be seen, tasted, felt, smelled, heard pre-purchase — virtual try-ons reduce uncertainty); **inseparability** (production and consumption simultaneous — frontline employees inseparable from delivery); **variability** (quality depends on who, when, where, how); **perishability** (cannot be stored — empty hotel rooms, unsold airline seats, lost concert tickets cannot be reclaimed) (Ch 11.1).

Lovelock's four service categories: people processing, possession processing, mental stimulus processing, information processing (Ch 11.1, Figure 11.6).

The **service-profit chain model** (Harvard 1990s): internal service quality → employee satisfaction → loyalty/productivity → external value proposition → customer satisfaction → customer loyalty → profit and growth (Ch 11.2, Figure 11.8). An employee feedback loop lets frontline employees communicate problems, because, per consultant Sidney Yoshida's study "The Iceberg of Ignorance," "4 percent of an organization’s frontline problems are known by top management, 9 percent are known by middle management, 74 percent are known by supervisors, and 100 percent are known by employees" [V] (Ch 11.2, "Steps in the Service-Profit Chain Model"). **Employee satisfaction** is "the level of happiness or contentment employees have with their jobs and work environment" [V], and is "often the direct result of company policies and support services that empower employees to deliver quality products and services" [V]; Zappos's Tony Hsieh, recognising that customer service staff were a customer's only person-to-person contact with an online retailer, encouraged his employees to go above and beyond for the customer [AP] (Ch 11.2, "Employee Satisfaction").
