SHRM estimate: 6–9 months of an employee's annual salary to replace [V]. Taco Bell case: high-retention restaurants had 2× sales and 55 per cent higher profits vs high-turnover stores [V].

The section's Marketing in Practice feature, "Ritz-Carlton", draws on a press source [BT, Toporek]. It defines **employee empowerment** as the ways an organisation gives its employees some autonomy and freedom to make decisions and some control over their day-to-day activities, as when a supermarket lets cashiers match competitors' ads up to a set dollar amount without a manager's approval [AP]. The Ritz-Carlton, “considered a gold standard for hospitality” [V], lets employees spend up to $2,000 to solve customer problems without manager approval [BT, Toporek]; the sum looks less surprising given that the customer lifetime value (CLV) of a Ritz-Carlton guest is $250,000 [BT, Toporek]. The box presents this empowerment as the hotel acting directly on its service-profit chain [AP] (Ch 11.2, "Ritz-Carlton").

The **Service Marketing Triangle** (three legs): external marketing (company → customer; making promises), internal marketing (company → employees; enabling promises), interactive marketing (employees → customers in **service encounters**; keeping promises) (Ch 11.2, Figure 11.10).

The **Gap Model of Service Quality** (1985, five gaps): knowledge gap (what customers expect vs what management thinks they expect); policy gap (management understanding vs service delivery policies and standards); delivery gap (specs vs actual delivery); communication gap (delivery vs what's communicated); customer gap (expectation vs perception of experience) (Ch 11.3, Figure 11.11).

The **RATER framework of service quality** (Zeithaml, Parasuraman, Berry): Reliability (3× more important than equipment or uniforms per research), Assurance (Mayo Clinic case — 500 original artworks, 70 US artists), Tangibles, Empathy, Responsiveness (Ch 11.3, Figure 11.12).

Ethics: Mintel — over half of US consumers stop buying from companies they perceive as unethical (Ch 11.4, "How Do Ethics Contribute to Customer Satisfaction").

The section's Companies with a Conscience feature, "Nasco Gulf", draws on the company's own Customer Service Code of Conduct [BT, Nasco Gulf]. As ethics grow more important to customers of services, the Dubai insurance agent focuses on trust as a way to build long-term loyalty [AP]. Its stated customer service mission is “to provide customers with timely, responsive service with integrity, simplicity, and a passion for excellence” [V], and its service principles are trust, understanding and resolve, the last put as “I solve our customer’s problems, even if the solution is difficult” [V]. Its published values are that its word is good, it is a bold partner, it works to earn loyalty, and it focuses on what matters [AP] (Ch 11.4, "Nasco Gulf").

## Part X: New product development (Ch 10)

### Five new-product categories and three innovation types

Five categories of "new" product: new-to-the-world (true inventions creating new markets); new-to-the-firm (gap-filling — Nature Valley granola bars); additions to existing product lines (Coca-Cola flavour variants); improvements/revisions to existing products (Meta's Oculus Quest 2 headset, an updated version of its original Oculus Quest); repositioned products (Bayer aspirin → heart attack prevention) (Ch 10.1, Figure 10.2).

Three innovation types by behavioural change: discontinuous (smartphones radically changing behaviour); continuous (Sony brighter TV — no behavioural change); dynamically continuous (PCs replacing typewriters — keyboard layout preserved) (Ch 10.1, "Customer Perceptions of Newness").

### Nine-stage NPD process

Nine stages: idea generation; idea screening and evaluation; concept development and testing (concept testing typically uses five-point Likert "definitely would purchase" through "definitely would not purchase"); market strategy development; business analysis (payback, break-even); product development (creating a **prototype**); test-marketing (sales-wave research; controlled test-marketing; full test-marketing — top US test cities are Nashville, Cincinnati, Indianapolis, Charleston SC, Jacksonville FL [V]; simulated test-markets; crowdsourcing); commercialisation; evaluation of results (Ch 10.2, Figure 10.3).

Maxwell House case: research showed consumers wanted "bold, vigorous, and deep tasting" coffee, but four months of formulation work showed it too expensive to produce; the cheaper formula didn't meet expectations and flopped (Ch 10.2, "Stage 6: Product Development").

The section's Careers in Marketing feature, "Product Development as a Career", notes that most companies have product manager (PM) as a job role, in which “you manage the product creation or further development” [V]. The rest of the box points to summaries of the role and its salaries, the skills and training it needs, sample PM job descriptions (Google, Meta, Twitter, Amazon) and the typical PM career path [AP] (Ch 10.2, "Product Development as a Career").

### Success and failure factors

Success factors: delivering unique benefits to users (5× success rate vs me-too products [V]); planning before development (well-defined predevelopment activities raised success rate from ~31 per cent to 75 per cent [V]); technological synergy; marketing synergy (2.3× success rate when present [V]); market attractiveness (Ch 10.4, Figure 10.5).

The section's Marketing in Practice feature, "Kentucky Fried Chicken (KFC)", draws on a press source [BT, Bond]. Although consumer spending typically spikes in the last six weeks of the year, KFC's sales typically falter then, since few people name fried chicken as holiday food [AP]. KFC's answer was a new product to keep the brand in mind over the holidays, the KFC 11 Herbs and Spices Firelog, which “when ignited, makes your house smell like fried chicken” [V]: a fireplace plays an important role in the holiday season, and the smell should make people want to eat fried chicken [BT, Bond]. Promotion through TV talk shows and magazines produced 5,000 user-generated social posts, and the logs sold out in three hours, which the box offers as a successful product launch [BT, Bond] (Ch 10.4, "Kentucky Fried Chicken (KFC)").

Failure factors: failure to understand consumer needs/wants (Google Glass discontinued 2015); targeting wrong market (Microsoft Zune chasing Apple iPod); lack of product point of difference (Google+ vs Facebook — shut down 2019); prolonged development/delayed market entry (Amazon Fire Phone 2014 — discontinued one year later); poor pricing/cost structure (Ch 10.4, Figure 10.7).

Christensen-attributed estimate: ~30,000 new products launched per year, 95 per cent fail [BT]; PDMA found failure rates 35 per cent (health care) to 49 per cent (consumer goods) [V] (Ch 10.4).

### Adoption process and Rogers's adopter categories

Five stages of consumer adoption: product awareness, product interest, product evaluation, product trial, product adoption (Ch 10.5, Figure 10.8). The book treats this as a "hierarchy of effects" and presents it alongside **diffusion of innovation** (Everett Rogers, 1962). Five characteristics affecting rate of adoption: relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, divisibility, communicability (Ch 10.5).

Diffusion was first thought a one-step process (mass media to the individual); marketers "now recognize that it is a two-step process" [V], the second step being **personal influence**, communication in which individuals affect others' purchasing decisions through their authority, knowledge, or position (Kylie Jenner, with over 250 million Instagram followers, is the example) [AP] (Ch 10.5, "Stages in the Adoption Process"). Rogers's five adopter categories: innovators, early adopters (the best target market for new innovations because they are "opinion leaders"), early majority, late majority (~34 per cent of population, will buy only after about half of population does), laggards (Ch 10.5, "New Product Adopter Categories").

### IP and ethics

**Patents** (20-year term in US); **copyrights** (original works of authorship — software, songs, TV shows, motion pictures); **trademarks** (word, phrase, symbol, design). Apple ordered to pay over $300 million to Personalized Media Communications LLC for patent infringement (March 2021) [V] (Ch 10.6).

The section's Companies with a Conscience feature, "Meta", draws on a press source [BT, McHugh]. Meta (formerly Facebook) came under fire after a whistleblower released internal research and documents and testified before the US Senate that the company “chooses profits over safety” [V]. To build ethics into its new product development, Meta hired Zvika Krieger to its Responsible Innovation Team (RIT); Krieger's role focused on ethical issues in both the engineering and the design processes, the RIT focused on identifying ethical issues at the design and development stage, and the RIT was involved, for example, in the decision to disallow filtering dating app results by race [AE]. Krieger left Meta and the RIT was dissolved in 2022, most members moving to other areas of the company, where they may be able to influence decisions more directly [AE] (Ch 10.6, "Meta").

## Part XI: Pricing (Ch 12)

### Price as value-indicator and the profit equation

The price-value equation: value = perceived benefits − perceived costs. Pricing must benefit both buyer (perceived value) and seller (profit-maximisation) (Ch 12.1, "Price as an Indicator of Value"). Profit = total revenue − total costs; total costs split into **fixed costs** (do not change with units produced) and **variable costs** (change with units produced) (Ch 12.1, "The Profit Equation").

The section's Marketing in Practice feature, "Upside", applies the price-value equation. Founded in 2016, Upside is an app that links users to gas stations, restaurants and grocery stores within a set radius; the user claims an offer, has four hours to upload the receipt, and is paid cash by businesses that have contracted with Upside to drive custom to them [AE]. The app “is banking on the value equation as well as psychological factors of pricing to attract both buyers and sellers” [V]: since gas prices barely vary between nearby stations, 25 cents a gallon cash back may lead a driver to give up the convenience of the closer station for a reward a few miles away, and the station gains a one-time or new customer [AE] (Ch 12.1, "Upside").

### Psychology of pricing

**Price anchoring** (Steve Jobs's iPad launch with $999 anchor before revealing $499 starting price); **artificial time constraints** (urgency-inducing); **price appearance** (longer, more syllabic prices feel more expensive — fancy restaurants use $29 not $29.00; study showed $1,555.83 perceived as complicated, $1555 simpler); **price gouging** (illegal in many jurisdictions — New York's 1978 law was the first state law of its kind; COVID-19 PPE list issued by US DOJ; Hurricane Katrina hotel manager sentenced to five years) (Ch 12.1, "The Psychology of Pricing").

The section's Careers in Marketing feature, "Pricing Analyst", defines the role: a pricing analyst “studies the market and analyzes data to determine the best pricing for products” [V]. The rest of the box points to job descriptions, a practitioner video, and articles on what makes a good pricing analyst and how the role differs from a data analyst [AP] (Ch 12.1, "Pricing Analyst").

### Five Cs of pricing and seven pricing objectives

Five Cs: cost, customers (Toyota vs Lexus segment positioning), channels of distribution (IKEA's manufacturer→dealer→wholesaler→retailer chain; a Link to Learning box, "IKEA", adds from a blog that IKEA has 1,600 suppliers manufacturing products for 186 global stores [BT]), competition, compatibility (with brand strategy — McDonald's $20 ribeye example as inappropriate) (Ch 12.2, Figure 12.3).

The section's Marketing in Practice feature, "The Five Cs of Pricing", notes that some practitioners add another consideration, **context**: “a more complex strategy of pricing where marketers set—and change—prices according to variables external to the company” [V]. An ice cream truck in the US Midwest would change its prices to fit the weather, with more traffic in peak summer hours and less in winter, while the product stays the same; whether the strategy fits depends on the product category, market size and other nuances of the industry [AE] (Ch 12.2, "The Five Cs of Pricing").

Five-step process: determine pricing objective, estimate demand, estimate costs, analyse external environment, select strategies/tactics (Ch 12.3, Figure 12.4).

Seven objectives (Table 12.1): customer value-based (GoToMeeting's $49 "all you can meet flat-rate pricing"); cost-based; sales-oriented (volume-driven); market-share-oriented (cell phone industry parity pricing); target return; competition-based (Amazon's algorithmic just-below-competitor pricing); customer-driven (what the customer is willing to pay; eBay auction model) (Ch 12.3, Table 12.1).

### Demand, elasticity, and the demand curve

The demand curve typically slopes downward: as price rises, quantity demanded falls. **Prestige pricing** is a notable exception: high price increases perceived value (Adidas Yeezy Boost 750 cost ~$76 to produce, sells for over $1,000) (Ch 12.3, "The Demand Curve for Prestige Products").

**Demand elasticity** = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price. Homes are elastic (many alternatives — apartments, roommates, condos); gasoline is relatively inelastic (few substitutes for car travel) — even with 2022 prices averaging over $5/gallon, demand remained relatively stable [V] (Ch 12.3, "Demand Elasticity"). Four factors: substitutes, income (income effect), time (e.g., automobile price drops produce delayed demand response), cross-elasticity of demand (coffee price up → tea demand up).

### New-product pricing strategies and existing-product tactics

Three new-product strategies: **price skimming** (initial high price, lowered over time — Sony PlayStation 3 from $599 to $299); **penetration pricing** (Netflix subscription); **break-even pricing** (covers costs but no profit; the break-even formula divides fixed costs by (unit price − unit variable cost) — 40,000 cookies needed to cover $20,000 fixed costs at $2 price, $1.50 variable cost) (Ch 12.4).

Existing-product tactics: product line pricing (Unilever brand tiers); captive product pricing (printer + ink); bundle pricing (fast-food meal); odd-even pricing (psychological — luxury uses even, budget uses odd); economy pricing (store brands vs name brands; Allegiant Air no-frills) (Ch 12.5).

### Pricing ethics

**Price fixing** (Audi/BMW/Buick/Chevrolet auto-parts class action); **deceptive price advertising** (FTC-regulated; "buy one get one free" with raised price beforehand); **predatory pricing** (Walmart accused by Wisconsin DATCP in 2000 of below-cost staples to drive out competition); **price discrimination** (legal if no specific economic harm); **monopoly gouging** (Texas 2020–2021 winter storm — $400/night Super 8 motel) (Ch 12.6).

The section's Companies with a Conscience feature, "Warby Parker", draws on the company's own history page and a press source [BT, Knowledge@Wharton]. Warby Parker set out to solve the problem of expensive eyeglasses, “a medical necessity for many people” [V], in an industry it described as “dominated by a single company that has been able to keep prices artificially high” [V]. Its answer was a direct-to-consumer approach and uniform pricing: every pair costs $95, against an average eyewear cost of $263, a spread that also made it hard for buyers to tell the value of a $200 pair from a $400 pair [BT, Knowledge@Wharton]. It makes glasses in-house, bypassing traditional supply chains, talks directly to customers about their needs, and donates one pair for every pair sold [AE] (Ch 12.6, "Warby Parker").

## Part XII: Integrated marketing communications (Ch 13–16)

### The promotion mix and its six elements

The **promotion mix** is the set of strategies marketers use to communicate with customers; six elements: advertising, sales promotion, personal selling, public relations, direct marketing, Internet/digital marketing (Ch 13.1, "Promotion Mix Defined"). Statista: $586 billion worldwide ad spending in 2020 [V] (Ch 13.1).

The section's Careers in Marketing feature, "Integrated Marketing Career", describes an IMC professional as one who "builds and manages campaigns that integrate all the facets of marketing" [V], naming advertising, public relations, digital campaigns and sales [AP]. The rest of the box is a pointer: it names educational organisations that specialise in integrated marketing (San Diego State University, Marist, Northwestern, Eastern Michigan University) and links to an article on the role's qualifications, experience and salary and to videos on IMC careers and the evolution of IMC (Ch 13.1, "Integrated Marketing Career").

### The communication process model

Sender → encoding → message → medium → receiver → decoding → feedback loop, all subject to **noise** (Ch 13.2, Figure 13.6). Marketers control sender, encoding, message, and medium; the rest is largely outside their control. Rule of thumb cited: 7–10 exposures needed before action [AP] (Ch 13.2, "Noise").

### IMC and the 5A framework

**Integrated marketing communications** (IMC) uses multiple promotion-mix methods to send the same message — better results, increased efficiency, improved brand awareness, repeated success, customer satisfaction (Ch 13.3). The **5A framework** maps the customer journey: Aware, Appeal, Ask, Act, Advocacy (Ch 13.4, Figure 13.10).

### IMC planning steps and message appeals

Steps: identify target audience; determine objectives (SMART); design the message; create message content; determine budget (objective and task, "perhaps the best method but is often used the least" [V]; top down; percent of sales; affordable; competitive parity); develop strategies and tactics; select promotional tools; design the promotion (message strategy, creative strategy, communication channel); schedule the promotion (continuous, flighting, pulsing); evaluate and measure (KPIs: ROI, cost per lead, cost per sale, conversion, engagement) (Ch 13.4).

Three message-appeal types: **rational** (Toyota alternative-fuel benefits); **emotional** (Coca-Cola "Happiness" campaign); **moral** (drink-driving public health). **Fear appeals** are a sub-type (smoking, vaccination) (Ch 13.4, "Create the Message Content").

The Emotional Appeals discussion carries a Link to Learning feature, "Happiness Campaign". Coca-Cola wanted to associate drinking a Coke with being happy and built a whole campaign on the emotion of happiness: "Everything in the campaign was focused on drinking Coke and choosing to be happy" [V]. It created the #choosehappiness hashtag for its social and digital promotions, and consumers posted pictures of themselves drinking a Coke with friends under it [AE]. The box links to a commercial from the campaign (Ch 13.4, "Happiness Campaign").

The Evaluate and Measure the Objectives step carries a Marketing Dashboard feature, "ROCI". It credits Don Schultz, named as the founder of IMC, with return on customer investment (ROCI) [BT, Schultz]: "a marginal analysis that shows the efficiency of marketing communications spending" [V]. The box argues that efficiency matters as much as effectiveness, and that ROCI weighs short- and long-term value through the change in profitability and value during the period and overall, tracking how revenue grows over time rather than in response to one campaign or action [AR]. Its ice cream shop example (period profit $38.00, change in customer value $10.00, starting customer value $21.00) gives an ROCI of $38.48, and the box says the measure finds the campaigns that yield the most profitable customers [AE] (Ch 13.4, "ROCI"; Table 13.1).

### Federal regulators

FTC (commercial speech, unfair methods, deceptive advertising); FCC (broadcast — radio, television, telephone); FDA (labelling, packaging, branding, ingredients lists, advertising — packaged foods, pharmaceuticals, cosmetics); CAN-SPAM Act (commercial email) (Ch 13.5, "Socially Responsible Marketing Communications").

The section closes with a Companies with a Conscience feature, "Farmer Direct Organic", drawn from the company's own "About" page [BT, Farmer Direct Organic]. A cooperative of farmers in Canada and the United States, it aims to grow better food and to change how consumers think about food and eat; its members focus on quality and transparency, and its food is 100 per cent organic and 100 per cent farmer owned [BT, Farmer Direct Organic]. Its social media showcases the family farms behind the food, and with a vision of a "food future that is good for you, for your family, for farmers, and for the planet" [V] it commits to pesticide monitoring, transparency and traceability from the store back to the farm [BT, Farmer Direct Organic] (Ch 13.5, "Farmer Direct Organic").

### Advertising types and budget approaches (Ch 14)

**Advertising** is "paid communication messages that identify a brand or organization and is intended to reach a large number of recipients" [V] (Ch 14.1, "Advertising and its Importance"). 2021 Super Bowl: $6 million per 30-second spot, 96.4 million viewers — ~6 cents per viewer cost-per-exposure (Ch 14.1).

Two ad classifications: **product advertisements** (specific product within mix; PepsiCo's Halloween Pepsi-with-Coke-cape vs Coca-Cola's "Everyone wants to be a hero"); **institutional advertisements** (whole organisation — Anheuser-Busch's COVID-19 hand-sanitiser pivot in 2020; 500K bottles delivered by April) (Ch 14.1).

Four advertising objectives: informative, persuasive, comparative (Wendy's "fresh never frozen"), reminder (Ch 14.2, "Establishing Advertising Objectives"). Push vs pull strategy. Five budget approaches (Table 14.1): percent of sales, all-you-can-afford, ROI, competitive parity, objective and task. The objective-and-task approach budgets from the objectives set for the advertising plan, but it "can lead to overspending when other factors are not considered" [V] (Ch 14.2, "Establishing the Advertising Budget").

Reach (estimated number of people reached); frequency (exposures per person per period); impact (how quickly received); engagement (interactions). Pretests: portfolio tests, jury tests, theater tests. Post-tests: aided recall, unaided recall, attitude tests, inquiry test, sales test (Ch 14.2).

### Advertising metrics and PR (Ch 14)

Brand recognition (logo→brand identification); brand awareness (recall information about brand); impressions = ratings × ads run × target audience size; conversion rate = converts ÷ audience × 100 (industry rule of thumb: 2–5 per cent traditional, 10 per cent+ digital is effective); ROAS = revenue ÷ ad spend (Ch 14.3).

The section's Marketing Dashboard feature, "Measuring the Impact of Advertising", introduces **cost per thousand** (CPM): "CPM is the cost to advertise to 1,000 people" [V], the "M" standing for the Latin *mille* [AP]. CPM rises with targetability, is higher for traditional media (television, radio, print, outdoor) than for digital, and may be higher for niche than for mass media [AP]. The box gives three criticisms: a view shows no intent to purchase or change in behaviour; views may be duplicated or mistargeted; and ads may fail to run or load [AR]. Its ice cream shop example ($1,000 for 2,000 impressions) gives a CPM of $500, and 15 customers at a $50 average lifetime value ($750) did not repay the $1,000 spend [AE] (Ch 14.3, "Measuring the Impact of Advertising").

**Public relations** is unpaid earned media, "creating and maintaining a favorable public image" (Ch 14.4). It has two sides: sharing positive stories about the organisation, and damage control through crisis communication. When PepsiCo aired a 2017 commercial, amid the height of the Black Lives Matter protests, in which Kendall Jenner calms an angry crowd by handing a police officer a can of Pepsi, activists criticised it for trivialising the issue; the company first defended the advertisement, then, after public backlash, apologised, saying it had "missed the mark" [V] [BT, Business Insider] (Ch 14.4, "Public Relations Defined"). Tools: press relations, public affairs, lobbying ($200+ million spent 2020 by top four lobbying associations: National Association of Realtors, US Chamber of Commerce, PhRMA, American Hospital Association [V]), events, digital/social media. Advantages: increased brand credibility (most credible/persuasive of all promotional forms), increased sales/leads, positive brand image, cost-effectiveness (Ice Bucket Challenge raised over $115 million worldwide for ALS [V]). Disadvantages: no direct control, lack of guaranteed results, difficulty evaluating effectiveness (Ch 14.5).

The section's Careers in Marketing feature, "Public Relations", defines a public relations professional as "someone who shares information on behalf of a company" [V] and notes that PR jobs come in various types, each needing particular skills [AP]. The rest of the box points to articles on PR job types and skills, on whether a PR career suits the reader and how to get one, and to a day-in-the-life video from a PR manager (Ch 14.4, "Public Relations").

The Tylenol 1982 cyanide-tampering case is the canonical PR-crisis exemplar: 30 million products recalled; "Johnson & Johnson faced the issue head-on" and won the trust of a nation (Ch 13.1, "Public Relations").

Ethical issues in advertising: truth in advertising (FTC laws against false claims; the watchdog group Truth in Advertising; Subway's "Eat Fresh" slogan challenged as misleading by its own franchisees in 2021); advertising to children (an estimated 40,000-plus commercials a year; Juul accused in 2019 of marketing to teens); and advertising harmful products, where organisations "can be held legally liable for the claims and for any harm caused by the product" [V] (Ch 14.6, "Ethical Issues Related to Advertising"). Ethical issues in public relations: transparency (Whole Foods' non-GMO verification after its mislabelling of genetically engineered foods); **selective truth telling**, "a practice in which a person or organization tells a portion of the truth but omits other portions of the truth" [V]; and verifying facts and information before release (Ch 14.6, "Ethical Issues Related to Public Relations").

The public relations ethics discussion carries a Link to Learning feature, "IKEA", drawing on Adweek [BT, Spary]. The COVID-19 pandemic led many companies to shift their marketing from selling goods and services to "creating feelings of goodwill and solidarity" [V]; early in the pandemic IKEA launched a campaign offering six ways to build a furniture fort, giving the public ways to cope with quarantine, and the campaign earned a nod in AdWeek's most notable advertisements [BT, Spary] (Ch 14.6, "IKEA").

The chapter's Companies with a Conscience feature, "TOMS", draws on an interview with founder Blake Mycoskie, the company's site and a WordStream post [BT, Mycoskie; TOMS; Shewan]. Mycoskie founded TOMS shoes in 2006, its name taken from the word "tomorrow"; the company is committed to a One for One model, donating an item to those in need for every item bought, and has committed one-third of its profits to grassroots movements [BT, Mycoskie; TOMS]. The box presents TOMS as a case of transparency: its behaviour is aligned with its values and every advertising campaign reinforces its philanthropic mission, so it is "nearly impossible for anyone to think of TOMS as anything but aligned completely with its mission" [V] [BT, Shewan] (Ch 14.6, "TOMS").

### Personal selling: the seven-step selling process (Ch 15)

Seven steps: prospecting and qualifying (developing **sales leads**, building a database, qualifying contacts); pre-approach (research); approach (rapport-building, soft); presentation (formats: stimulus-response, formula selling using AIDA — attention/interest/desire/action, need/satisfaction, adaptive selling, consultative selling à la Miracle on 34th Street); handling objections; closing (often the hardest step; trial closes via financial-terms or delivery-timing questions); follow-up ("After the order is placed, the real work begins" [V]; lifetime customer value) (Ch 15.3).

Salesperson roles: **order takers** (inside, outside); **order getters**; support personnel (missionary salespeople — pharmaceutical detailers; technical specialists); team selling. Sales force structure: territorial, product, customer (industry). Compensation methods: commission only; salary only; salary + commission; salary + individual bonus; salary + commission + bonus (Ch 15.2, Ch 15.4).

The section's Careers in Marketing feature, "Personal Selling", defines personal selling as "a technique used by sales professionals to make a connection and possible sale with customers" [V] and points readers to articles on selling techniques, the kinds of sales jobs and job titles, and the sales skills employers value [AP]. It describes a sales career as "fast-paced, exhilarating, and competitive" [V] and advises anyone interested to research positions and industries until they find one they are passionate about [AP] (Ch 15.2, "Personal Selling").

### Sales promotion (Ch 15)

Sales promotion: **consumer-oriented** (pull) — coupons, samples, premiums, contests (analytical/creative skills), sweepstakes (chance — Publishers Clearing House $1M cash prize; magazine purchase not necessary), loyalty programs, point-of-purchase displays, rebates (reimbursement once the consumer submits proof of purchase by a deadline; consumers often fail to claim them because the process seems too laborious [AP]); **trade-oriented** (push) — allowances and discounts, cooperative advertising (Publix advertises Boar's Head with Boar's Head co-op funding), cash bonuses, credit terms, dealer conferences, push incentives (Ch 15.6).

The section's Marketing Dashboard feature, "Cost of Customer Acquisition", reminds readers that profitability must also count the cost of acquiring customers, and that both selling (salary or commission) and sales promotion create such costs [AP]. What is acceptable depends on the product: thousands of dollars of sales effort can be reasonable for a multimillion-dollar airplane, but the cost to acquire a buyer of several-hundred-dollar televisions "must be much lower" [AE]. Cost of acquisition is the total cost of marketing activities divided by the number of customers acquired; because the formula assumes every customer is worth the same, which marketers know is untrue, campaigns need a variety of metrics [AP]. In the worked example (Table 15.1), $4,650,000 of promotion yields 810,000 customers, or $5.74 each, which the box judges worth spending for a bookseller whose customers bring $90 of profit on average over their lifetime [AE] (Ch 15.5, "Cost of Customer Acquisition").

The section's Marketing in Practice feature, "Domino’s", shows companies using special days such as National Coffee Day, National Pet Adoption Day and National Pizza Day to focus attention, create a news story and boost sales or donations in the short term [AE]. Pizza delivery companies use sales promotion to cope with a highly competitive industry [AP]. For National Pizza Day 2022, Domino’s, known for fast delivery, ran an unusual promotion that gave consumers $3 back for picking up their pizza instead of having it delivered [BT, Breen]: "The $3 coupon was redeemable the following week on another carryout order of $5 or more before tax and gratuity" [V] (Ch 15.6, "Domino’s").

The section's Companies with a Conscience feature, "Tentree", draws on the company's own statements [BT, Tentree]. The sustainable clothing brand runs typical consumer-oriented promotions, such as a percentage off for newsletter sign-ups, but also plants 10 trees for every purchase, which gives consumers an incentive to buy [BT, Tentree]. Its Facebook page frames the pledge with the line "big change starts small" [V] and says planting 10 trees per purchase aims "to make big change accessible to everybody" [V]. The company had planted over 81 million trees and set a goal of 1 billion by 2030 [BT, Tentree] (Ch 15.7, "Tentree").

The **Pareto principle** for marketing as introduced earlier: "80 percent of a company's revenue comes from the top 20 percent of repeat or loyal customers" [V] (Ch 5.1, "Behavioral Segmentation").

### Direct, online, social media, and mobile marketing (Ch 16)

Traditional direct marketing forms: direct-mail (Casper, Warby Parker have added direct mail; average mail life 17 days [V]); catalog (Lands' End, IKEA — response rates jumped 170 per cent over the last decade per HBR 2020 [V]); telemarketing (call centers; National Do Not Call Registry 2003); direct-response TV/DRTV (Dollar Shave Club's Michael Dubin video — 27 million views; Proactiv 2020 sales $1 billion [V]); seminars; trade shows (CES, MailCon) (Ch 16.1).

Online direct marketing: website marketing (Apple, Amazon transactional; Bleacher Report community); email marketing (4 billion daily users; 99 per cent of people check email daily [V]); content marketing (Dotdash Meredith); online video (a Link to Learning box relays Wyzowl's 2022 survey: 86 per cent of businesses use video as a marketing tool, 94 per cent of companies believe videos help customers better understand their product, and 99 per cent of video marketers will keep using it [BT, Wyzowl] (Ch 16.1, "Wyzowl’s Survey Found on HubSpot")); blogs (HubSpot's blog drives traffic to its CRM/marketing platform); online forums.

The section's Careers in Marketing feature, "Digital Marketer", sums up the role in one line, digital marketers "build and implement a company’s online-related activities and sales" [V], and points readers to a Glassdoor job description and to guides from Ahrefs, Neil Patel, the Digital Marketing Institute, Indeed and Emerson College on starting a digital marketing career, getting a first job without experience, and the most sought-after roles [AP] (Ch 16.1, "Digital Marketer").

"In segments under the age of 30, the most popular platforms are Instagram, Snapchat, and TikTok" [V] (Ch 16.2, "Social Media Marketing"). Social media platforms covered: Facebook (2.9 billion monthly active users, $117.92 billion revenue; criticised over personal-data use; six in ten social media users have observed and temporarily believed false info on Facebook [V]); Instagram (1 billion monthly active; #yearwrapped Spotify Stories 60 million users engaged, 3 billion playlists streamed); LinkedIn (722 million members; 73 per cent agree LinkedIn protects privacy — most-trusted social media platform [V]); Pinterest (478 million monthly users; 97 per cent of searches are unbranded — favourable for advertisers); Twitter (238 million daily active; 67 per cent of B2B businesses use); podcasts (200 per cent year-on-year growth; Spotify acquired Megaphone 2020; 52 per cent of listeners trust advertising endorsed by host [V]) (Ch 16.2).

Mobile strategy: responsive web design (Google prioritised mobile-friendly in 2015); mobile-friendly emails (68 per cent of emails opened on mobile [V]; subject lines 41–50 chars); app development; short/memorable URLs. A Link to Learning box relays Oberlo's forecast that US mobile advertising spend will grow 14 per cent to $156 billion in 2023 and reach $174 billion in 2024 [BT, Oberlo] (Ch 16.2, "US Mobile Advertising").

The section's Marketing in Practice feature, "National Geographic", presents the brand as a visual storyteller with over 220 million Instagram followers, the leading brand account on the site [BT, National Geographic Partners]. Its Wanderlust campaign invites amateur photographers worldwide to post their best travel photographs under the #wanderlustcontest hashtag [BT, Oxford], and the book calls this promotion of user-generated content "a great way to connect with followers and build continuous engagement" [V]. On days such as Endangered Species Day and Oceans Day it pushes wildlife and nature-protection content central to the brand's values [BT, Nat Geo Wild], and social media lets it engage followers "in a personal way" [V] (Ch 16.2, "National Geographic").

Online metrics: website traffic; traffic by source (paid search, organic search, paid social, affiliates); conversions; bounce rate (target < 40 per cent); search trends; new vs returning visitors; average session duration; page views; most-visited pages; social engagement; **click-through rate** (CTR); **cost per click** (CPC); **cost per acquisition** (CPA = total marketing cost ÷ customers acquired) (Ch 16.3).

The section's Marketing Dashboard feature, "Targeted Advertising", explains that targeted advertising lets marketers specify an audience of their choosing, as when a recent search for winter boots brings ads for winter boots [AE]. Because it is tailored to the marketer's exact specifications it can be expensive, so marketers calculate the cost each time a prospect clicks an ad: cost per click is the total digital campaign cost divided by the number of clicks, and it also applies to ads served on a search engine results page [AP]. Since "not every click results in a purchase" [V], marketers should not invest more in clicks than profitability allows and should weigh average revenue and profit per order and customer lifetime value [AP]. In the pet-store example (Table 16.1), the bird-feeder campaign works out at $1.10 per click; a shopper who clicked through placed a $70 order at a 10 per cent margin, and the box, asking whether "the click-through rate" was a good investment, answers yes: the store "profited $7 on the single purchase at a click-through rate of just $1.10" [V] [AE] (Ch 16.3, "Targeted Advertising").

Ethics: privacy (KPMG: 86 per cent growing concern, 78 per cent fear data collection [V]; 75 per cent want more transparency); Apple iOS app-tracking opt-in popups disrupting Facebook/Google ad models (Ch 16.4).

The section's Companies with a Conscience feature, "Apple’s Taking Big Steps to Protect Privacy", draws on Apple support pages and press sources [BT, Apple; Kaczanowski]. In January 2022 Apple introduced iCloud Private Relay, which hides a user's IP address from the websites they visit, "essentially masking a user’s entire online footprint" [V]; the book calls it a game changer for digital marketing because companies like Meta and Google depend on seeing a consumer's online journey to serve relevant messages [AP]. Apple also released Hide My Email, which forwards mail sent to a randomly generated address so the user's real address stays hidden, and changed its Mail app to stop marketers tracking whether an email was opened, a measure email marketers use to gauge engagement [BT, Apple; Kaczanowski]. The box concludes that Apple is equipping consumers to protect their personal information and "navigate the web unseen" [V] (Ch 16.4, "Apple’s Taking Big Steps to Protect Privacy").

## Part XIII: Distribution, retailing, wholesaling (Ch 17–18)

### Marketing channels and intermediary functions

A **marketing channel** is "a system of people, organizations, and activities that work together to make goods and services available to consumers to purchase" [V] (Ch 17.1, "Marketing Channels Defined"). Four intermediary types: agents/brokers (never take possession; commission/fee); distributors (Coca-Cola distributors only carry Coca-Cola products); wholesalers (bulk-purchase, bulk-break); retailers (smallest quantities to end consumers).

Three intermediary functions: transactional (buying, selling, risk-bearing); logistical (handling, packing, inventory, transport, warehousing, security); facilitating (financing, sharing information). Intermediaries reduce transaction count: 9 → 5 in the 3-manufacturers × 3-customers example (Ch 17.1, Figure 17.3). Other value-adds: providing information; **bulk-breaking**; **accumulating** across producers; adjusting for **discrepancy of assortment**; providing customer credit.

The section's Careers in Marketing feature, "Distribution Management", says distribution managers "determine when, where, and how much of a product is distributed" [V]. It points readers to a Michigan State University career profile (sample job description, roles and responsibilities, salary, education and training) [AP] and relays ZipRecruiter's finding that, of the several skills the role needs, compliance and customer service are the most common [BT, ZipRecruiter] (Ch 17.1, "Distribution Management").

### Channel types and conflict

Direct (manufacturer → consumer; pizza shop) vs indirect (with one or more intermediaries). Industrial channels parallel consumer with agents and distributors representing producers; Element Fleet Management (Toronto-based, manages corporate fleets across United States, Canada, Mexico) is cited.

Marketing systems: **conventional** (each member maximises own profit); **vertical marketing system (VMS)** — corporate (Walmart's Equate brand), administered (P&G coordinating without ownership), contractual (franchise — Chipotle, McDonald's); horizontal (J.Crew + New Balance); multichannel (Nike: physical stores, Nike.com, Amazon, Kohl's, Foot Locker); omnichannel (Dick's Sporting Goods buy-online-pickup-in-store, kiosk-buy-deliver) (Ch 17.2, Figure 17.7).

Selected channel members must be continuously managed and motivated: "The qualities of an effective channel relationship include collaboration, transparency, and cohesion" [V]; manufacturers reinforce channel-member performance with incentives such as bonuses and other rewards, and support members with helpful sales materials, product samples, and the right messaging [AP] (Ch 17.4, "Managing and Motivating Channel Members"). Channel conflict: vertical (between levels — **disintermediation** as a special case: iTunes destroyed traditional music outlets); horizontal (within level — Holiday Inn locations) (Ch 17.4, "Handling Channel Conflict").

### Channel choice factors

Target market coverage: intensive (Coca-Cola, Kraft); selective (Whirlpool, GE through Lowe's, Home Depot dealer network); exclusive (Rolex). Buyer requirements: information (in-store demos at Whole Foods; Ace Hardware "the helpful place"); convenience; variety (Petco, PetSmart); pre/post-sale service. Product factors: unit value; perishability; bulk and weight; standardization; technical nature; product life-cycle stage; profitability (Ch 17.3).

### Channel performance metrics

Inventory turnover rate; order accuracy rate (e-commerce critical); time to ship (Amazon-set expectations); total units in storage (with **SKUs** — stock-keeping units); total number of orders; percentage of on-time shipments (Chobani example for perishables); average delivery days (Ch 17.4, Figure 17.11).

### Supply chain management and logistics

**Supply chain management** = "managing all the members and activities from the procurement and transformation of raw materials into finished goods through their distribution to targeted consumers" (Ch 17.5). Five SCM functions: purchasing, operations (forecasting demand to align inventory and production), logistics, resource management, information workflow. Dave's Killer Bread is cited as starting its value-promise far back in the supply chain via certified-organic suppliers.

Logistics functions: warehousing (receiving, storing, picking, packing, shipping; temperature control where needed); inventory management; transportation. Five transportation modes (Table 17.2): trucking (moderate speed, low cost, high accessibility); rail (slow, low cost, moderate accessibility); water (very slow, very low cost, moderate accessibility); air (fast, very high cost, low accessibility); digital (very fast, very low cost, very high accessibility) (Ch 17.6).

The chapter's ethics section carries a Companies with a Conscience feature, "Allbirds", drawn from the company's "Renewable Materials" web page [BT, Allbirds]. It says the footwear industry "has missed the opportunity to look to Mother Nature for more sustainable footwear materials" [V], with most shoe companies using petroleum-based raw materials [BT, Allbirds]. Founder Tim Brown, with product engineer Joey Zwillinger, developed a wool fabric designed for footwear; Allbirds also uses SweetFoam, a sole material made from plant-based leather, and recycled synthetics where needed to extend product life [BT, Allbirds]. Its stated goals are to double the lifetime of its products and cut the carbon footprint of its raw materials by 25 per cent in 2025 [BT, Allbirds]; the feature closes that "Sustainability is at the core of everything Allbirds does" [V] (Ch 17.7, "Allbirds").

### Retailing types and strategy (Ch 18)

Retailing is "the process of selling goods and services to consumers" — the final stop in the channel (Ch 18.1). Functions: provide assortment, buy in bulk, store inventory, provide convenience (location and hours — Walmart 24-hour stores), provide services (banking, pharmacy, hair salon), collect/provide feedback.

Ten store-retailer types (Table 18.1): specialty store (single line — AutoZone); department store (JCPenney, Kohl's); supermarket (Publix — ~32,000 sq ft, ~50 per cent grocery, ~50 per cent household/personal); convenience store (~150,000 in US in 2020 [V]; first 7-Eleven 1927 Texas); superstore (Target — 1,927 stores per cited count); category killer (Best Buy, Lowe's, Home Depot, Staples, Office Depot); discount store (Dollar General, Dollar Tree, Family Dollar); off-price retailer (T.J.Maxx, Ross — irregulars/closeouts/overstock); factory outlet (Sawgrass Mills with 350+ stores — largest in US); warehouse club (Costco, Sam's Club, BJ's — paid membership).

Six non-store types: automatic vending (Carvana 27th car vending machine in Atlanta in 2020 — 12 stories, 43 vehicles [V]); direct mail/catalogs (Tiffany's Blue Book 1845 — first US mail-order catalog; Sears "big book" final edition 1993); television home shopping (QVC — generated $14.1 billion 2018 [V]; acquired HSN 2017); online retailing ($5.4 trillion US online retail spend 2021 [V]; expected to reach 22 per cent of global retail by 2023); telemarketing (FTC 1991 rules; 2003 Do Not Call Registry); direct selling (Kirby B2C, publishing/tech B2B).

Retail strategy: **markup** (retail − purchase price ÷ purchase price × 100; **keystone pricing** doubles wholesale; grocery ~15 per cent, clothing 100–300 per cent [V] (Ch 18.3, "Retail Pricing")); maintained markup; markdowns; gross margin = net sales − COGS. Locations: central business district ("Manhattan is the world’s largest central business district"; "It has the highest retail rent in the world" [V] (Ch 18.3, "Central Business District")); regional shopping center/mall (Mall of America — retailtainment); strip mall; freestanding location.

Two Link to Learning features point to the same video on the expansion of dollar stores. In 18.2, "Dollar Stores and the Community" says the impact of dollar stores on community and commerce is "not always positive" [V], with experts in the video discussing potential negative impacts [AP] (Ch 18.2, "Dollar Stores and the Community"). In 18.3, "Success in Small Towns" says that with the rise of large retailers such as Walmart, mom-and-pop stores have struggled to compete in recent decades, an economic problem for small towns and rural areas, but some retailers are finding new success locating there, with dollar stores finding a niche in towns where many other retailers have closed [AP] (Ch 18.3, "Success in Small Towns").

Retail trends: social commerce (Macy's ambassador program — 5 per cent commission to outside influencers; social commerce grew 30 per cent 2019–2020 [V]); online stores in offline spaces (Walgreens drive-through pickup of online orders); same-day delivery (Kozmo.com 1998 pioneer; defunct 2001; revived by Amazon Prime); digital wallets (touchless payments) (Ch 18.4).

### Wholesaling

Three merchant-wholesaler tiers: **full-service** (most risk; general-merchandise/full-line; specialty wholesaler — Sysco for food service); **limited-service** (rack jobbers — gas-station phone-charger displays; cash-and-carry; drop shippers — never take possession; truck jobbers — perishables); **manufacturer's agents/representatives** (independent contractors selling for multiple manufacturers; never take possession) (Ch 18.5, Figure 18.15).

Wholesaling trends and ethics: growing competition; global supply-chain pressures (COVID-19 shortages of workers, products, containers, long-haul drivers); regulatory complexity (Sale of Goods Act); consumer protection (caveat emptor displaced by consumer protection); product traceability (USDA 2022 ground-beef recall — 25,000+ pounds traced to specific location, date, lot) (Ch 18.6).

The section's Link to Learning feature, "Traceability Standards", adds that the GS1 Global Traceability Standard "defines what is minimally acceptable for full supply chain traceability" [V] and sets up a system that traces products end to end, with an application to food [BT, GS1] (Ch 18.6, "Traceability Standards").

The chapter's ethics section carries a Companies with a Conscience feature, "Trader Joe’s", drawn from a press source [BT, Seely]. The chain, first opened in Pasadena, California, in 1967, has 505 stores in over 42 states plus an online presence, and "has always been committed to improving sustainability in its channel" [V]. Unlike many grocery competitors it donates 100 per cent of its unsold products; it bars certain controversial products from the manufacture of its private-label goods, makes organic products more accessible, has removed more than 6 million pounds of plastic from packaging, and keeps high rates of employee satisfaction [BT, Seely]. Its ethical decisions involve relationship building along the supply chain so that each channel member upholds high ethical standards, and the feature names Natural Grocers, Sprouts, Costco and Whole Foods as other supermarkets known for ethical practices [BT, Seely] (Ch 18.7, "Trader Joe’s").

## Part XIV: Sustainable marketing as the new paradigm (Ch 19)

### The three pillars and ESG framing

**Sustainable marketing** (Kotler): "an organization should meet the needs of its present consumers without compromising the ability of future generations to fulfill their own needs" [BT] (Ch 19.1, "Environmental Sustainability"). Three pillars / "planet, people, and profits": **environmental** (Stonyfield Organic 30 per cent emissions reduction by 2030 commitment; Subaru of Indiana Automotive recycles or composts 98 per cent of manufacturing waste, remaining 2 per cent waste-to-fuel [V]); **social** (Adobe diversity/equity/inclusion programs); **economic/governance** (profitability + business ethics; voting governance, legal compliance, accounting standards). The text aligns these with **ESG strategy** — environmental, social, governance — as the standard reporting and accountability frame (Ch 19.1, "Environmental Sustainability"; Ch 19.2, "Differences between Traditional and Sustainable Marketing").

The section's Link to Learning feature, "The Story behind State Bags", gives a social-pillar example of a company that works to support its community: State Bags donates a bag filled with school supplies for each bag purchased and partners with nonprofits such as Seeds of Peace, Time's Up, and Bottomless Closet to support women and children from underserved communities [BT, State Bags] (Ch 19.1, "The Story behind State Bags").

IBM consumer-behaviour study: 57 per cent of consumers would alter consumption habits to be more environmentally conscious; ~80 per cent indicated sustainability is essential [V] (Ch 19.1).

### Traditional vs sustainable marketing

Traditional marketing takes a customer approach (4Ps for a target audience). "Sustainable marketing takes a “stakeholder approach” and considers customers, shareholders, employees, vendors, interest groups, media, and the general public" [V] (Ch 19.2, "Differences between Traditional and Sustainable Marketing"). Costco: "Sustainability to us is remaining a profitable business while doing the right thing" [BT] (Ch 19.2). **Corporate social responsibility (CSR)** holds that companies have an obligation to use their platforms to improve the world and not cause harm.

The section's Link to Learning feature, "Costco Sustainability Commitment", notes that Costco publishes its commitment to sustainability on its website "as a way to be fully transparent about its sustainability strategy" [V], sharing its code of ethics, mission statement, sustainability principles and responsibilities, and development goals [AE] (Ch 19.2, "Costco Sustainability Commitment").

### Benefits, principles, and purpose-driven marketing

Benefits: enhanced brand recognition (Patagonia repairs goods, donates 1 per cent of annual sales, Action Works activism platform); reduced costs (Bain & Company: 5× revenue growth among brands scoring highest on sustainability [V]; Ben & Jerry's removed plastic straws/spoons); improved effectiveness (Mastercard saw avg annual profit growth of nearly 19 per cent in the 10 years it connected purpose to profits [V]); easier compliance with regulators (going beyond legal obligations); waste minimisation (McDonald's goal of 100 per cent guest packaging from renewable/recycled/certified sources by 2025); enhanced ROI (Ch 19.3).

The section's Link to Learning feature, "Anya Hindmarch and Antidote", says Anya Hindmarch's "I Am Not a Plastic Bag" campaign was a collaboration with the creative agency Antidote "that gained loads of press coverage" [V], and that the publicity contributed to the U.K. decision to charge for plastic bags [AE]. It also points to the designer's later collection of biodegradable leather bags [AP] (Ch 19.3, "Anya Hindmarch and Antidote").

Five sustainability marketing principles: consumer-oriented marketing (Zappos extensive customer-service team); customer-value marketing (Tiffany & Co. luxury); innovative marketing (Shedd Aquarium 2020 virtual penguin field trip); **mission-driven marketing** (charity: water — Scott Harrison's storytelling); **societal marketing** (Athleta Power of She campaign — ~70 per cent of apparel from recycled/sustainable materials [V]) (Ch 19.4).

The section's Link to Learning feature, "Charity: Water", reports that charity: water has raised more than $640 million and funded more than 91,000 water projects in 29 countries, and points to a video in which founder Scott Harrison tells his personal experience of the impact of dirty water, as an example of his storytelling [AE] (Ch 19.4, "Charity: Water").

Purpose-driven brands: Accenture global survey of 30,000 consumers — 62 per cent want companies to take a stand on sustainability/transparency/fair working conditions [V] (Ch 19.5). Bombas 5 million+ items donated through 3,500+ impact partners. Dove Campaign for Real Beauty as multi-decade purpose campaign. Walmart 2022 Juneteenth ice cream as cautionary example of inauthentic purpose-marketing backlash.

The section's Link to Learning feature, "Dove’s Campaign for Real Beauty", lists three of the campaign's commercials: Real Beauty Sketches, which "artistically compares the gap between self-perception with perception from others" [V]; the anti-photoshopping film Evolution, a viral behind-the-scenes look at what happens with beauty ads; and Reverse Selfie, on the impact of social media on young girls' self-esteem [AE]. It says that seeing how companies focus on purpose will help readers' creativity in future marketing jobs, and points to two articles on why the campaign succeeded [AP] (Ch 19.5, "Dove’s Campaign for Real Beauty").

## Positions the text explicitly frames against

- *Product-driven strategies* (the production concept's "If you build it, they will come", Ch 1.4): framed against in favour of customer-driven strategy (Ch 1.1).
- *"One size fits all"* generic strategies: framed against; generalising buyers anywhere in the world "is a shortsighted perspective, because it limits business growth and commercial possibilities" (Ch 8.2).
- *Caveat emptor*: framed as an outdated motto displaced by consumer-protection regulation (Ch 18.6).
- *Marketing-as-advertising-or-sales-only* (a layperson conflation): framed against early in the text (Ch 13.1).
- *Production concept and product concept eras*: framed as historically superseded by the marketing concept and societal marketing concept (Ch 1.4).
- *Marketing myopia* (railroad example): framed as a cautionary tale (Ch 1.4).
- *Conventional channel systems* (each member self-maximising): framed against in favour of vertical marketing systems (Ch 17.2).
- *Shareholder-only obligation*: framed as the traditional view, displaced by a stakeholder-CSR-ESG view (Ch 19.2).
- *Customer-only focus in marketing* (rather than stakeholder approach): framed as traditional, displaced by sustainable marketing (Ch 19.2).
- *Inauthentic purpose-marketing*: framed against — the Walmart 2022 Juneteenth ice cream example (Ch 19.5).

## Citation and source-integrity notes

- **Conversion path:** this reference was read from a pymupdf4llm 0.2.9 conversion, which lost page anchors (hence section-name citations) and dropped framed feature boxes; the source has since been re-converted (2026-10-16, PyMuPDF text blocks; see the source card). On 2026-10-17 the spans that re-conversion restored were listed by an order-aware word diff of the old and new conversions (runs of 8 or more inserted words), checked against the old text so moved text did not count, and read in full; the Coverage line records what was added.
- **Coverage:** substantive content only (Option B per repo policy). Excluded scaffolding sections per chapter (Chapter Outline, Chapter Summary, Key Terms, Applied Marketing Knowledge: Discussion Questions, Critical Thinking Exercises, Building Your Personal Brand, What Do Marketers Do?, Marketing Plan Exercise, Closing Company Case, References) and the back-matter (Preface "About OpenStax" through "Coverage and Scope", Answer Key, Index).
- **Source materials:** read in full from `corpus.commons/demo/sources/converted/openstax-principles-marketing.md` (41,595 lines; ~2 MB). All chapters' substantive sections were read. The text is highly pedagogical (each section ends with a Knowledge Check); the Knowledge Check question prompts are excluded from the deep ref but were used as confirmation cues for concept identification.
- **Spelling preservation:** OpenStax verbatim quotes preserve American spelling; the deep ref's surrounding prose uses British spelling per repo convention.
- **Hofstede dimensions count discrepancy:** the text presents *four* dimensions in Ch 5.3 (PDI, IDV, UAI, MAS) and *six* dimensions in Ch 8.3 (adding long-term/short-term orientation and indulgence/restraint). This reflects Hofstede's evolving framework; both presentations are recorded as the source presents them.
- **Multiple definitions of "noise" and "feedback"**: the text uses these terms in both the communication-process model (Ch 13.2) and elsewhere; meanings are consistent within each context.
- **No fabricated examples or training-data filling:** every named company example, statistic, and citation in this deep reference traces to a passage in the source markdown.
